stem: Child fell from tree, vomiting, head swelling, he became drowsy. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE management?
why_right: A child who fell from a tree, is vomiting and has "become drowsy" has a deteriorating level of consciousness after head injury. Trauma care follows ABC, so securing the airway (intubation) to protect against aspiration and hypoxia comes before any definitive neurosurgical step. The hematoma has not even been confirmed on CT yet.
why_wrong_block: A. Hematoma evacuation: needs a CT showing a surgical lesion (e.g. epidural hematoma with midline shift) and a secured airway; it becomes the answer when the stem already gives that CT and the airway is not the problem.
key_concept:
Head injury with falling consciousness: Airway first, then CT, then surgery.
  • Intubate: GCS 8 or less, unconscious, SpO2 below 88%, or aspiration risk (vomiting with drowsiness)
  • Then non-contrast CT head
  • Epidural hematoma: lens-shaped, middle meningeal artery, lucid interval
  • Surgical hematoma with mass effect: craniotomy and evacuation
exam_pearl: When the stem gives no CT and only symptoms of deterioration, the answer is the airway; when it gives CT with midline shift and a stable child, the answer is evacuation.

stem: 12/16 years old girl fall 2 meters while playing, The loss of consciousness then vomited many times and then become sleepy, in examination there is head hematoma and left limb weakness and sign of lateralization, CT brain show extra dural hematoma with midline shift. ( no GCS in the Qs) What is the best next management?
OptD: repeat the CT scan after 12 hours.
highlight_terms_source: left limb weakness and sign of lateralization
extra dural hematoma with midline shift
why_right: Fall from 2 meters, loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, sleepiness, "left limb weakness" and lateralizing signs with CT showing an "extradural hematoma with midline shift" means a surgical lesion with mass effect. The definitive and time-critical treatment is urgent craniotomy and hematoma evacuation; midline shift over 5 mm is an accepted indication.
why_wrong_block:
B. Intubate and secure the airway: the first step when GCS is 8 or less or the airway is at risk, and it may be done on the way to theatre, but no GCS is given and the question has already reached the CT stage; the decision being tested is surgery.
C. Admit and observe: right for a small epidural hematoma without midline shift or neurological deficit in an alert patient; focal weakness and shift rule it out.
D. Repeat CT after 12 hours: right for a minor stable lesion being monitored; waiting with lateralizing signs and shift risks herniation and death.
key_concept:
Epidural hematoma: arterial bleed that needs evacuation once it causes mass effect.
  • Source: middle meningeal artery (temporal fracture)
  • CT: biconvex, lens-shaped
  • Clinical: lucid interval, ipsilateral blown pupil, contralateral weakness
  • Midline shift over 5 mm or focal deficit: craniotomy and evacuation
  • Small, no shift, alert: observe with repeat CT
exam_pearl: CT already showing shift plus lateralizing signs moves the answer from airway or observation to evacuation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Short version: child fell from 2 meters, vomiting multiple times and sleepy, left side weakness, CT shows extradural hemorrhage; options hematoma evacuation (highlighted) vs intubate and secure the airway. Related: Hematoma with 6mm midline shift -> Craniotomy. Midline shift > 5mm -> Craniotomy.

stem: 7-year-old child presents with recurrent tonsillitis (six episodes in the past year), snoring, mouth breathing during sleep, and has grade three tonsils. What is the most appropriate management option for this patient?
highlight_terms_source: recurrent tonsillitis (six episodes in the past year)
why_right: This 7-year-old has obstructive sleep-disordered breathing (snoring, mouth breathing during sleep) with grade 3 tonsils, plus recurrent tonsillitis (six episodes in one year). Six episodes alone falls just short of the strict Paradise threshold, but sleep-disordered breathing is both an independent indication and a modifying factor that favours surgery. In an otherwise healthy child whose large tonsils explain the symptoms, adenotonsillectomy is the most appropriate management and first-line treatment of paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea.
why_wrong_block:
A. Family counselling is part of any plan but does not treat obstruction or recurrent infection; it is the answer when no surgical criteria are met.
B. Stopping medication has no role; no drug is causing the problem, and repeated antibiotics are the reason surgery is considered.
D. A sleep study (polysomnography) is required before surgery when the child has comorbidities (obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial or neuromuscular disease) or when tonsil size and symptoms do not match; here the picture is clear-cut.
key_concept:
Paediatric tonsillectomy indications.
  • Recurrent throat infection (Paradise): ≥7 episodes in 1 year, ≥5/year for 2 years, or ≥3/year for 3 years
  • Obstructive sleep-disordered breathing with tonsillar hypertrophy
  • Peritonsillar abscess recurrence
  • Suspected malignancy (asymmetric tonsil)
  • PSG first only if comorbid or symptoms and exam disagree
exam_pearl: Snoring plus big tonsils in a healthy child: go to adenotonsillectomy; a sleep study comes first only when the case is unclear or the child is high risk.

stem: 28-year-old patient presented to the clinic complaining of perianal discharge. He reported history of on-off abdominal pain. He reported family history of Crohn's disease. On examination, three fistula openings at 3, 7 and 9 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 28-year-old with "three fistula openings", recurrent abdominal pain and a family history of Crohn's has multiple, complex perianal fistulae that point to undiagnosed Crohn's disease. This recall's key is colonoscopy (with ileoscopy and biopsies) to confirm the underlying disease, because fistula management is very different in Crohn's (medical therapy, setons, avoiding fistulotomy).
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI: the gold-standard imaging to map fistula tracts and find abscesses; it is the answer when Crohn's is already known and the question asks for fistula anatomy or a suspected abscess.
C. Fistulogram: an older, less accurate way to outline a tract, largely replaced by MRI and endoanal ultrasound.
D. US: endoanal ultrasound can assess simple tracts and sphincters, but transabdominal US does not diagnose Crohn's or map complex perianal disease.
key_concept:
Multiple or recurrent perianal fistulae: think Crohn's.
  • Suspected Crohn's not yet diagnosed: colonoscopy with ileoscopy and biopsy
  • Fistula anatomy or abscess: MRI pelvis
  • Abscess: drain before escalating immunosuppression
  • Fistulizing Crohn's: anti-TNF (infliximab), setons
  • Simple low non-Crohn's fistula: fistulotomy
exam_pearl: Known Crohn's with perianal sepsis: MRI pelvis; suspected but undiagnosed Crohn's: colonoscopy.

stem: Case for new born I forgot what he have but the ph low and hypokalemia? Urine pH 6.5
why_right: Low blood pH with hypokalaemia and a urine pH of 6.5 means the kidney cannot acidify the urine despite systemic acidosis. Inability to lower urine pH below 5.5 during acidosis is the defining feature of distal (type 1) RTA, where distal H+ secretion fails; it also wastes potassium.
why_wrong_block:
A. Proximal (type 2) RTA also causes hypokalaemia, but once serum bicarbonate falls the intact distal tubule can still acidify urine below 5.5. Right when urine pH is acidic during steady-state acidosis, or with Fanconi features.
B. There is no "medial" RTA; the recognised types are 1 (distal), 2 (proximal), 3 (rare mixed) and 4 (hyperkalaemic). This is a made-up distractor.
D. Fanconi syndrome is generalized proximal tubule failure (glycosuria with normal blood glucose, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia) causing a proximal RTA, so urine can still be acidified. Right when the stem lists those extra urinary losses or rickets.
key_concept:
All RTAs: non-anion-gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Separate by urine pH and potassium:
  • Type 1 (distal): urine pH > 5.5, low K, stones/nephrocalcinosis
  • Type 2 (proximal): urine pH < 5.5 once HCO3 is low, low K, Fanconi association
  • Type 4: urine pH < 5.5, HIGH K (aldosterone deficiency or resistance)
exam_pearl: Acidosis with an alkaline urine (pH > 5.5) = distal; if potassium is high instead of low, think type 4.

stem: Female patient with Lt hearing loss and tinnitus, autophony with preserved stapedial reflex, on examination normal tympanic membrane, diagnosis.
key_concept:
Normal TM + hearing symptoms: use the reflex.
  • Otosclerosis: conductive loss, stapedial reflex ABSENT
  • Superior canal dehiscence: pseudo-conductive loss, reflex PRESERVED, supranormal bone conduction, Tullio sign
  • Patulous Eustachian tube: autophony with breathing sounds, positional relief, TM moves with breathing, hearing usually normal
  • Weber lateralises to the affected ear in conductive or third-window loss
exam_pearl: Air-bone gap with an intact stapedial reflex is not otosclerosis; think third-window lesion.

stem: Regarding febrile convulsions in children, which of the following statements is correct?
OptA: There is 2% chance to develop epilepsy
OptB: Anti epileptic medication daily will reduce the risk
OptC: Antipyretic during fever will reduce the risk of future epilepsy
OptD: The child will have intellectual disability
key_concept:
Febrile seizure: age about 6 months to 6 years with fever, benign prognosis.
  • Epilepsy risk after simple FS: about 1 to 2%
  • Higher with complex FS, abnormal development, family history of epilepsy
  • Antipyretics: comfort only, no preventive effect
  • Daily antiepileptics: not recommended, no effect on later epilepsy
  • No long-term cognitive sequelae
exam_pearl: Any option claiming that antipyretics or daily drugs reduce future epilepsy, or that the child will have intellectual disability, is a myth.

Compiler note: No highlight; compiler placed '??' after option A.

stem: Regarding febrile convulsions in children, which of the following statements is correct?
OptA: There is a 2% chance to develop epilepsy
OptB: If it is a complex febrile seizure, it is more likely to progress to epilepsy
OptC: If parents had febrile seizures, it will increase the chance to progress to epilepsy
OptD: Using antipyretics will decrease the chance of febrile convulsions
why_right: Febrile seizures are generally benign, but the risk of later epilepsy rises when the seizure is complex (focal, longer than 15 minutes, or recurring within 24 hours). Complex features are one of the main risk factors for epilepsy, along with abnormal neurodevelopment and a family history of epilepsy, so B is the reliably true statement.
why_wrong_block:
A. A risk of about 1 to 2% applies only to simple febrile seizures; stated as a fixed figure for all febrile seizures it ignores the higher risk with complex seizures, so it is weaker than B.
C. A parental history of febrile seizures raises the chance of the child having febrile seizures and recurrences, not epilepsy. It is a family history of EPILEPSY that increases the epilepsy risk.
D. Antipyretics make the child comfortable but have not been shown to prevent febrile convulsions or their recurrence.
key_concept:
Simple vs complex febrile seizure:
  • Simple: generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours
  • Complex: focal, over 15 minutes, or repeated within 24 hours
  • Epilepsy risk factors: complex FS, abnormal development, family history of epilepsy
  • Recurrence risk factors: young age at first seizure, family history of febrile seizures, low fever at seizure
exam_pearl: Family history of febrile seizures predicts recurrence; family history of epilepsy predicts epilepsy. Do not swap them.

stem: Newborn of diabetic mother with jittery movements. Asked About Management:
why_right: An infant of a diabetic mother has fetal hyperinsulinism that persists after birth, so glucose falls quickly. Jittery movements make this symptomatic hypoglycaemia until proven otherwise: check a bedside glucose and give IV dextrose (a 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose bolus followed by a continuous infusion). Symptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia is treated intravenously, not with feeding or waiting.
why_wrong_block:
A. IM glucagon is a temporary rescue when IV access cannot be obtained; it is not the first-line treatment when IV dextrose can be given.
B. Feeding is appropriate for an asymptomatic or mildly low glucose. Once the baby is symptomatic (jittery), oral feeding is too slow and unreliable.
C. Waiting delays treatment of symptomatic hypoglycaemia and risks seizures and permanent brain injury.
key_concept:
Neonatal hypoglycaemia ladder:
  • At risk, asymptomatic: early feeding and glucose monitoring
  • Symptomatic (jittery, lethargy, poor feeding, seizure): IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus then infusion
  • Peripheral line limit 12.5% dextrose; higher needs central access
  • No IV access: IM glucagon as a bridge
exam_pearl: Jitteriness in an infant of a diabetic mother is hypoglycaemia first; if glucose is normal, then check calcium (and consider polycythaemia).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option notes by compiler: A IM glucagon, if after 72 hours we think hypocalcemia; B oral breast feeding, no benefit; C waiting 2 hours (not sure), no benefit. Infant of diabetic mother + jittery = symptomatic hypoglycemia = IV dextrose immediately; we should check blood sugar. Maternal hyperglycemia crosses placenta, fetal hyperinsulinemia persists after birth causing rapid hypoglycemia; jitteriness, tremors, lethargy, poor feeding, seizures are symptoms. Any jittery newborn = hypoglycemia until proven otherwise; if symptomatic do not wait or rely on feeding: IV dextrose ✅ bolus D10W 2 mL/kg then continuous infusion. Oral breastfeeding only for asymptomatic/mild hypoglycemia. Waiting 2 hours is dangerous: brain injury, seizures, permanent neurologic damage.

stem: A 3-day-old full-term infant presents with episodes of jitteriness and brief seizures lasting a few seconds that resolve spontaneously. Laboratory results are reported as normal; however, the glucose level was not provided. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
key_concept:
Neonatal seizure approach:
  • First: bedside glucose; correct hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose
  • Then: calcium, magnesium, sodium; sepsis work-up as indicated
  • Persistent seizures with metabolic causes corrected: phenobarbital first line
  • Jitteriness stops with gentle restraint; seizures do not
exam_pearl: When a stem says labs are normal but glucose was not given, the missing glucose is the point: check it and treat it first.

stem: concerning and warrants further evaluation for possible malignancy. Which of the following types of nipple discharge is most concerning?
OptD: Spontaneous unilateral, from a single duct, and clear
why_right: Pathological nipple discharge is "spontaneous", "unilateral" and from a "single duct", and is usually serous (clear) or bloody. These three features suggest a localized ductal lesion (intraductal papilloma or carcinoma) and need imaging and evaluation whatever the colour. The other options each have a feature that makes them physiological or benign.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spontaneous and bilateral red: blood is worrying, but bilateral, multi-duct discharge suggests a systemic or diffuse benign process; unilateral single-duct bloody discharge would be the concerning version (classically intraductal papilloma).
B. Spontaneous bilateral milky: galactorrhea from prolactin excess, drugs, pregnancy or lactation; it needs a prolactin and drug review, not a malignancy work-up.
C. Induced unilateral green: discharge produced by squeezing, especially green or dark, is typical of duct ectasia or fibrocystic change and is benign.
key_concept:
Nipple discharge red flags: spontaneous, unilateral, single duct, bloody or serous.
  • Physiological: bilateral, multi-duct, expressed only, milky or green
  • Bloody single duct: intraductal papilloma most common cause
  • Green/dark with inverted nipple: duct ectasia
  • Milky bilateral: galactorrhea (check prolactin, drugs, pregnancy)
  • Pathological pattern: imaging (US with or without mammogram), then biopsy or duct excision
exam_pearl: Colour alone does not make discharge malignant; spontaneity, laterality and single-duct origin do.

stem: child was riding a bicycle, and then he sustained a handlebar injury, he presented to the ER with abdominal pain and tenderness And Nausea & Vomiting FAST Was Done And It Was Inconclusive. What’s Most Likely Injured Abdominal Organ?
highlight_terms_source: FAST Was Done And It Was Inconclusive
why_right: A "handlebar injury" is a focused blow to the epigastrium that crushes the pancreas (and duodenum) against the vertebral column, classically in children. The pancreas is retroperitoneal, so FAST is often "inconclusive" because early free intraperitoneal fluid may be absent; CT abdomen with contrast is the test when this is suspected.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spleen: the most commonly injured solid organ in blunt abdominal trauma overall, with left upper quadrant pain and usually free fluid on FAST; the handlebar mechanism points elsewhere.
B. Liver: commonly injured in right upper quadrant blows and usually produces hemoperitoneum visible on FAST.
D. Urinary bladder: injured with pelvic fractures or a blow to a full bladder, presenting with hematuria or inability to void, not an epigastric handlebar impact.
key_concept:
Mechanism predicts organ in blunt trauma.
  • Handlebar (epigastric) blow: pancreas and duodenum
  • Retroperitoneal injury: FAST may be negative or inconclusive
  • Suspected pancreatic or duodenal injury, stable: CT abdomen with contrast
  • Lap belt: small bowel, mesentery, lumbar (Chance) fracture
  • Overall most common solid organ: spleen
exam_pearl: "Most commonly injured organ" in blunt trauma is spleen, but a handlebar mechanism with negative FAST is pancreas.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: C. Pancreas ✅ (also highlighted; 'Soft tissue' written beside C). Handlebar injury (direct epigastric blow) causes pancreatic injury, especially in children. FAST is often inconclusive because pancreatic injuries are retroperitoneal and may not produce significant free intraperitoneal fluid early. UpToDate, ATLS (may not be detected on FAST; CT abdomen with contrast if suspected), Nelson.

stem: A diabetic patient presents with a NON-HEALING foot ulcer. The patient complains of numbness. On exam, The ulcer shows central erythema. (no mention of "with signs of healing", no mention of pulse). He's unable to perceive touch and sensation. What is the most critical test to perform to reach the diagnosis?
why_right: The stem already shows neuropathy ("numbness", "unable to perceive touch"), so the open question for a "NON-HEALING" diabetic ulcer with no pulse findings given is whether the limb has enough blood supply. Peripheral arterial disease is the main reason a diabetic ulcer fails to heal, and the ABI is the critical bedside test for it; it decides referral for revascularization and whether the wound can heal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Monofilament test: screens for loss of protective sensation; it is the answer for routine diabetic foot screening, but here the sensory loss is already evident and does not explain failure to heal.
C. Assessment of pressure points: important for offloading and preventing ulcers, but it does not diagnose the cause of a non-healing ulcer.
key_concept:
Non-healing diabetic foot ulcer: check perfusion first.
  • First step: palpate pulses, then ABI
  • ABI 0.9 to 1.4: normal; below 0.9: PAD; below 0.5: severe
  • ABI above 1.4: calcified vessels (common in diabetes), use toe pressures or Doppler
  • Absent pulse: arterial Doppler; intact pulse with dark skin: venous duplex
  • Monofilament: annual neuropathy screening
exam_pearl: In diabetics a falsely high ABI from calcified arteries can hide PAD; that is when toe pressures or Doppler are used.

stem: A 12-year-old presents with left sided lower abdominal pain. Examination confirms a slightly elevated, tender left testis with redness and edema of the scrotum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 12-year-old with lower abdominal pain and a slightly elevated, tender testis has testicular torsion: the twisted cord pulls the testis upward, and adolescent torsion commonly refers pain to the lower abdomen. Redness and edema of the scrotum come from venous congestion. The alternate recall adds an absent cremasteric reflex and no transillumination, which point the same way.
why_wrong_block:
B. Epididymo-orchitis has a gradual onset with fever or urinary symptoms, a preserved cremasteric reflex and pain relieved by elevation; the testis is not high riding. Think of it in a sexually active young man, or in a child with a UTI or urinary tract anomaly.
C. An incarcerated inguinal hernia is a tender, irreducible lump that extends from the scrotum up into the groin, typically in an infant; here the finding is an elevated tender testis, not a groin mass.
D. Torsion of a testicular appendage gives tenderness localized to the upper pole (blue dot sign) with a normally positioned, vertical testis; the whole testis being elevated and tender points to true torsion.
key_concept:
Acute scrotum: decide by testis position, reflex and site of tenderness.
  • Torsion: sudden, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex
  • Appendage torsion: upper pole tenderness, blue dot, vertical testis
  • Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, fever, dysuria, reflex present
  • Incarcerated hernia: irreducible tender lump into the groin
  • Torsion: urgent exploration, imaging must not delay surgery
exam_pearl: Vertical testis with focal upper pole tenderness flips the answer to appendage torsion; an elevated whole testis keeps it at torsion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): sudden hemiscrotal pain with swelling and tenderness, cremasteric reflex absent, no transillumination (didn't mention 'high riding'): A testicular torsion (highlighted), B epididymo-orchitis, C hydrocele.

stem: Elderly women with previous laparotomy for sigmoidectomy after complicated diverticulitis, with incisional hernia symptomatic painful What is the best next step?
why_right: An incisional hernia after a previous laparotomy that is symptomatic and painful needs repair, and incisional hernias are repaired with mesh because suture repair alone has a high recurrence rate. A laparoscopic approach with mesh reinforcement gives a lower wound infection rate and faster recovery, which suits an elderly patient with a scarred abdomen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance is only for a small asymptomatic hernia in a patient unfit or unwilling for surgery; this hernia is painful, so it should be repaired.
B. Open repair without mesh (primary suture) has an unacceptably high recurrence for incisional hernias; tissue repair is reserved for very small defects or a contaminated field where mesh is avoided.
C. Laparoscopic repair is the right approach, but without mesh it is incomplete: the laparoscopic incisional repair is by definition a mesh repair, so the option that names the mesh is the best answer.
key_concept:
Symptomatic hernia = repair; incisional hernia = mesh.
  • Laparoscopic mesh indications: bilateral, recurrent, need for fast recovery, incisional/ventral
  • Primary unilateral inguinal hernia in a fit patient: open mesh repair
  • Suture repair alone: high recurrence for incisional hernias
  • Strangulated or obstructed hernia: emergency surgery
exam_pearl: When one option says repair and another says the same repair with mesh, the mesh option wins for an incisional hernia.

stem: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn TTN pedia patient he was started on O2 and but still has mild respiratory distress. O2 sat 96%. How to feed.. RR is 65 ?
OptD: IV fluids and avoid oral feeding
highlight_terms_source: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn TTN
why_right: TTN is a self limiting failure to clear fetal lung fluid, so the baby only needs support until it resolves. With a RR of 65 and mild distress despite O2, oral feeding is unsafe because the tachypneic infant cannot coordinate suck, swallow and breathe and may aspirate. The gut is normal, so enteral feeding should continue: nasogastric (gavage) feeds of expressed breast milk give nutrition without aspiration risk.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral expressed breast milk: right milk, wrong route. Oral feeding is resumed once the respiratory rate settles and the baby can feed without distress; at RR 65 it risks aspiration.
C. TPN: reserved for babies who cannot use the gut for a prolonged period (e.g. extreme prematurity, NEC, gut failure). TTN resolves within days and the gut works.
D. IV fluids and nil by mouth: chosen when distress is severe (marked tachypnea, rising O2 need, impending ventilation). This baby has only mild distress with SpO2 96%, so enteral NGT feeds are preferred.
key_concept:
Feeding a tachypneic newborn scales with the severity of distress.
  • Mild tachypnea, feeding comfortably: oral / breastfeed
  • Moderate tachypnea or mild distress: NGT (gavage) feeds
  • Severe distress, high O2 need or ventilation: NPO + IV fluids
  • TTN: term, C-section, fluid in fissures on CXR, resolves in days
  • RDS: preterm, surfactant deficiency, ground glass CXR
exam_pearl: Persistent tachypnea with mild distress means bypass the mouth (NGT), not the gut; save NPO + IV for severe distress.

stem: A 3-year-old his mother is concerned that he does not interact or play with other children and prefers to play alone. The boy can speak [3- To 4 word Phrases (Literally Written Like This) ], jump, walk on his toes, run draw a rough circle, can’t draw figures,pour water into a cup, and follow complex commands. What is the most likely assessment of his development?
highlight_terms_source: does not interact or play with other children
why_right: Check each domain against age 3. Gross motor (jumps, runs), fine motor (rough circle, pours water) and language (3 to 4 word phrases, follows complex commands) are all on track. The only abnormal domain is social: he does not interact or play with other children and prefers to play alone, whereas a 3-year-old should be playing interactively with peers. An isolated social interaction deficit points to a psychosocial / social communication disorder that warrants autism screening.
why_wrong_block:
A. Gross motor delay: he jumps, runs and walks normally, which is age appropriate. Would apply if a 3-year-old could not climb stairs or run.
C. Normal development: motor and language are normal, but avoiding peer play at 3 years is not; a 3-year-old should have moved beyond solitary play.
D. Fine motor delay: drawing a rough circle and pouring water are appropriate; drawing a person or a square comes later (4 to 5 years), so being unable to draw figures is expected.
key_concept:
Assess development domain by domain; the abnormal domain names the answer.
  • 3 y gross motor: alternates feet on stairs, jumps, tricycle
  • 3 y fine motor: tower of 8 blocks, circle
  • 3 y language: 3 word sentences, 75% intelligible to strangers
  • Square at 5 y, person with 3 parts at 4 y
  • Social: pretend play at 2 y, interactive play with peers by 3 y
  • Isolated social deficit with normal motor and language: screen for autism
exam_pearl: Normal motor and speech do not make development normal; a 3-year-old who will not play with peers has a social domain problem.

stem: A 9-year-old boy who has nighttime enuresis 3 times a week and has never been dry . His urine CX and analysis are normal, and his PE is unremarkable. What should he do next?
why_right: A 9-year-old who has never been dry has primary nocturnal enuresis; normal urinalysis and culture and an unremarkable exam make it monosymptomatic with no organic cause. At this age it is no longer something to just wait out, so first line treatment is behavioural: limiting evening fluids, voiding before bed, a reward chart and an enuresis alarm (desmopressin is the drug alternative).
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI lumbar spine: only when there is a lumbosacral deformity, abnormal neurological exam or daytime symptoms with constipation suggesting a spinal defect; his exam is normal.
B. Referral to urology: needed for daytime symptoms, recurrent UTI (renal US and VCUG) or failure of first line therapy, not for uncomplicated monosymptomatic enuresis.
D. Reassure: appropriate in a younger child (under about 5 to 6 years), when bedwetting is still developmentally normal. At 9 years with frequent wetting, treatment is offered.
key_concept:
Nocturnal enuresis work up: UA for all, then classify.
  • Primary (never dry) vs secondary (dry, then relapse: look for stress, UTI, DM)
  • Normal UA + no daytime symptoms: monosymptomatic, treat with behavioural measures / alarm
  • Desmopressin: alternative or for short term needs
  • Recurrent UTI: renal US + VCUG
  • Spine deformity or abnormal neuro exam: MRI spine
  • Young child: reassure
exam_pearl: Age flips the answer: reassure the young child; treat with behavioural therapy / alarm once school aged.

stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought by his mother because she is concerned he might have contracted chickenpox after close contact with a child with chickenpox 2 days ago. What is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: close contact with a child with chickenpox 2 days ago
why_right: Post exposure prophylaxis depends on immune status. This is a healthy 12-year-old exposed 2 days ago, with no vaccination or past chickenpox mentioned, so he is treated as non immune (unknown status). For an immunocompetent contact who is unvaccinated or of unknown status, varicella vaccine given early after exposure (ideally within 3 to 5 days) can prevent or modify the illness and also gives lasting immunity.
why_wrong_block:
A. Acyclovir: treats established varicella (IV in immunocompromised or high risk patients); it is not the first line prophylaxis for a healthy exposed child when the vaccine can be given.
B. IVIG (varicella zoster immunoglobulin): for exposed people who cannot receive a live vaccine, such as immunocompromised children, pregnant women without immunity and certain newborns.
D. Observe: correct if the child is already immune (vaccinated or past infection). Here immunity is not established, so prophylaxis is due.
key_concept:
Varicella post exposure prophylaxis by immune status.
  • Immunocompetent, vaccinated / immune: observe
  • Immunocompetent, unvaccinated or unknown: varicella vaccine (early after exposure)
  • Immunocompromised, asymptomatic: VZIG
  • Immunocompromised, symptomatic: IV acyclovir
  • Pregnant without immunity: VZIG (live vaccine contraindicated)
exam_pearl: Same exposure, different host: healthy child gets vaccine; leukemia on chemo gets VZIG.

stem: A 5 year old boy known case of leukemia, on chemotherapy and steroids for 6 weeks, presented to the clinic with his parents as he had contact with a child who has chickenpox, What to do?
highlight_terms_source: contact with a child who has chickenpox
why_right: This child is immunocompromised (leukemia on chemotherapy and steroids) and is a contact with no symptoms yet. He is at high risk of severe disseminated varicella, and a live vaccine is contraindicated, so passive immunisation with varicella zoster immunoglobulin is given as soon as possible after exposure.
why_wrong_block:
B. Admit and give acyclovir: IV acyclovir is for an immunocompromised child who has already developed varicella (symptomatic); he is only an asymptomatic contact.
C. Chickenpox vaccine: live attenuated, so contraindicated during chemotherapy and high dose steroids; it is the answer only for a healthy, non immune contact.
D. Stop chemotherapy: not part of post exposure management; interrupting leukemia treatment adds risk and does not prevent infection.
key_concept:
Varicella exposure: decide by host, then by symptoms.
  • Healthy, immune: observe
  • Healthy, non immune: vaccine
  • Immunocompromised, asymptomatic: VZIG
  • Immunocompromised, symptomatic: admit + IV acyclovir
  • Live vaccines (varicella, MMR) contraindicated on chemotherapy / high dose steroids
exam_pearl: Exposure without symptoms in an immunocompromised child = immunoglobulin; rash or symptoms = IV acyclovir.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: recall inside the 68 block; immunocompromised variant with a different answer from 68.

stem: A 8 months old baby, exclusively breastfeeding came with reduction in weight at birth he was 50th percentile now after month she is at 10th percentile, his height and head circumference still in 50th percentile.
highlight_terms_source: height and head circumference still in 50th percentile
why_right: Weight has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile, crossing two major centile lines, while length and head circumference stay on the 50th. A weight only drop with preserved growth of length and head points to inadequate caloric intake rather than an organic disease. At 8 months breast milk alone no longer meets energy needs (complementary foods should start around 6 months), so the advice is to increase calorie intake.
why_wrong_block:
A. Metabolic disorder: suspected when growth failure is global (length and head also falling) or with vomiting, lethargy, acidosis or developmental regression; here only weight is affected and the infant is otherwise well.
C. Reassure: crossing two major percentile lines is not a normal fluctuation and needs action; reassurance fits physiological early weight loss or small shifts within a centile channel.
key_concept:
Pattern of growth failure points to the cause.
  • Weight falls first, length and head preserved: inadequate intake (nutritional)
  • Weight and length both down, head preserved: endocrine or genetic short stature
  • All three down including head: congenital, genetic or CNS cause
  • Exclusive breastfeeding to about 6 months, then add complementary foods
  • Weight gain slows to about 10 to 15 g/day at 6 to 12 months
exam_pearl: Exclusively breastfed past 6 months with weight only centile drop: the fix is more calories (start solids), not a metabolic work up.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): 8 month old exclusively breastfeeding, weight 50th then 10th percentile, parent worried, advice to prevent further decline: A Improve caloric intake (highlighted), B Weight fluctuation is normal at this age, C metabolic screening, D Reassurance.

stem: A 4 months old baby, exclusively breastfeeding came with reduction in weight at birth he was 50th percentile now after month she is at 10th percentile, his height and head circumference still in 50th percentile. Her parent is worried, What advice to give the parent to prevent further decline in weight?
key_concept:
Weight only centile fall with preserved length and head suggests a nutritional cause.
  • Crossing ≥2 major centile lines: abnormal, needs action
  • Weight down, length and head preserved: inadequate intake
  • Head and length also down: think organic, genetic, CNS
  • Exclusive breastfeeding is appropriate until about 6 months
  • Expected gain 3 to 6 months: about 20 g/day
exam_pearl: Decide how far the weight has dropped: one channel can be reassured, two major lines with spared length and head means feeding is inadequate.

Compiler note: Both B and C are highlighted; compiler note: 'B but I'm stilling not sure'.
Other marked answers: Compiler highlight: C. Reassure

stem: history of vomiting and diarrhea. His mother reports decreased oral intake and increasing lethargy over the past 12 hours. On examination, he is drowsy but arousable, and his breath has a fruity (nail polish-like) odor. Vital signs reveal mild hypotension. Laboratory results show: Random blood sugar (RBS): 8.9 mmol/L Serum sodium: 131 mmol/L, Bicarbonate: 15 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause of his current condition?
why_right: This recall's key is DKA because the child has vomiting, lethargy, hypotension (dehydration), a fruity (nail polish like) breath from acetone and a low bicarbonate of 15, the ketotic acidosis picture. Among the options DKA is the only diagnosis that accounts for ketones plus metabolic acidosis; the other options name a single lab finding or a non ketotic state.
why_wrong_block:
B. Uncontrolled hyperglycemia: describes a glucose number, not the cause of the acidosis and fruity breath; and RBS 8.9 mmol/L is not markedly high.
C. Hyponatremia: sodium 131 is a mild consequence of vomiting and diarrhea, not the cause of drowsiness and ketotic breath.
D. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: needs very high glucose and high osmolality with little or no ketosis; here glucose is near normal and the breath is ketotic.
key_concept:
DKA needs hyperglycemia + acidosis + ketosis.
  • Clinical: vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, lethargy, fruity breath, Kussmaul breathing.
  • Labs (ISPAD 2022): pH < 7.3 or HCO3 < 18, ketonemia or ketonuria, glucose > 11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL).
  • HHS: very high glucose and osmolality, minimal ketones.
  • Ketosis with normal glucose after poor intake: starvation ketosis.
exam_pearl: Fruity breath means ketones; check the glucose before calling it DKA.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Stem is truncated in the source (begins mid-sentence).

stem: Baby after delivery went into respiratory distress, abnormal breathing pattern, tachypnea, saturation 78% , there were some meconium stains around the baby. What's next step?
OptC: Intubation and mechanical ventilation if needed
why_right: This recall's key is intubation because the newborn is non vigorous: respiratory distress with an abnormal breathing pattern, SpO2 78% and meconium staining suggest meconium aspiration. The source's reasoning follows the older approach to a distressed meconium stained baby: secure the airway (intubate, suction below the cords) and ventilate if needed, rather than giving oxygen alone or waiting for investigations.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxygen: free flow O2 or CPAP is for a baby who is breathing but remains hypoxic or labored; in this recall's logic the abnormal breathing pattern with meconium calls for airway control first.
B. Observation: acceptable only for a vigorous meconium stained baby with normal breathing, tone and heart rate; this baby is distressed and hypoxic.
D. ABGs: useful later to guide ventilation, but obtaining a gas must not delay airway and breathing support in an unstable newborn.
key_concept:
Neonatal resuscitation: airway and breathing first, investigations later.
  • Vigorous meconium stained baby: routine care, observe
  • Non vigorous: initial steps (warm, position, clear airway, stimulate)
  • Apnoea, gasping or HR < 100: positive pressure ventilation
  • Labored breathing or persistent cyanosis: SpO2 monitoring, O2, consider CPAP
  • PPV ineffective or prolonged ventilation needed: intubate
  • Routine tracheal suctioning for meconium is no longer recommended
exam_pearl: Meconium plus a distressed, hypoxic newborn: act on airway and breathing first, never observe or wait for a gas.

stem: Teenage girl sits on her ipad a lot and keeps comparing herself with others, she has low self esteem and anxiety, what’s the most she could benefit from?
OptB: Force her to leave social media
why_right: The teenager has low self esteem, anxiety and keeps comparing herself with others on her iPad: the problem is a pattern of negative thoughts, not severe depression. Cognitive behavioral therapy targets exactly these distorted comparisons and beliefs, and psychological therapy is first line for mild to moderate anxiety and low mood in adolescents.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antidepressant: kept for moderate to severe depression or anxiety, or when psychological therapy fails or is unavailable; not first for low self esteem with mild anxiety.
B. Force her to leave social media: coercive, damages rapport and does not address her thinking pattern; it is likely to be refused or resented.
C. Limit social media time: reasonable supportive advice, but it removes a trigger rather than treating the underlying anxiety and low self esteem.
key_concept:
Adolescent anxiety or low mood: therapy first, drugs second.
  • Mild to moderate: CBT (or other talking therapy).
  • Moderate to severe or failed therapy: add an SSRI (fluoxetine in adolescent depression).
  • Screen use advice is supportive, not the main treatment.
exam_pearl: "Comparing herself with others" is a cognitive distortion, which is what CBT is built to fix.

stem: Old female + Weight loss & Stool +ve for occult blood + Constipation
why_right: An older woman with weight loss, change in bowel habit (constipation) and a positive fecal occult blood test has colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. A positive occult blood test always needs a full colonoscopy, which views the entire colon, allows biopsy and detects synchronous lesions.
why_wrong_block: A. Sigmoidoscopy only examines the rectum and sigmoid, so a right sided (proximal) tumor, which often presents with occult bleeding and anemia, would be missed. Even when sigmoidoscopy finds a distal cancer, a full colonoscopy is still required to look for synchronous tumors.
key_concept:
Positive FOBT or red flags (age, weight loss, bowel habit change, iron deficiency anemia) = colonoscopy.
  • Colonoscopy: whole colon, biopsy, synchronous lesions
  • Cancer found on sigmoidoscopy: next step colonoscopy, then CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging
  • Iron deficiency anemia in an older adult: upper and lower GI endoscopy
  • Multiple liver lesions with constitutional symptoms: colonoscopy to find the primary
exam_pearl: Occult blood plus weight loss is never followed up with a limited scope; the answer is the full colonoscopy.

stem: A 7 month old pediatric came with convergence and esotropia.and during exam absent corneal light reflex The parents are concerned what should you do?
why_right: A 7-month-old with "convergence and esotropia" and an abnormal corneal light reflex (Hirschberg test) has true strabismus, not pseudostrabismus. Intermittent misalignment is common only in the first few months; a constant deviation at this age needs ophthalmology referral to look for an underlying cause (refractive error, cataract, retinoblastoma) and to prevent amblyopia.
why_wrong_block: A. Reassurance fits pseudostrabismus, where broad epicanthal folds make the eyes look crossed but the corneal light reflex is symmetric and centered; here the reflex is abnormal, so the strabismus is real.
key_concept:
Infant eye turning: the corneal light reflex decides.
  • Symmetric centered light reflex: pseudostrabismus, reassure
  • Asymmetric or displaced reflex: true strabismus, refer to ophthalmology
  • Esotropia: reflex displaced temporally; exotropia: displaced nasally
  • Most serious complication of untreated strabismus: amblyopia
  • Always check the red reflex too (cataract, retinoblastoma)
exam_pearl: Reassure only when the corneal light reflex is symmetric; any persistent true strabismus beyond early infancy goes to ophthalmology.

stem: 2-Month-Old Infant Presents To Vaccination Clinic. What Are The Recommended Vaccines According To National Program?
OptC: IPV, HBV, DTP, HIB, PCV, Rota
why_right: At the 2-month visit the Saudi national schedule gives IPV, DTaP, hepatitis B, Hib, PCV13 and rotavirus. Option C is the only list containing all six, with no vaccine that belongs to a later visit.
why_wrong_block:
A. IPV, HBV, DTP, HIB, MMR: includes MMR, a live vaccine first given at 12 months, and omits PCV and rotavirus.
B. IPV, HBV, DTP, HAV, PCV: includes hepatitis A, which is given at 18 and 24 months, and omits Hib and rotavirus.
D. IPV, HBV, DTP, HIB: incomplete, missing PCV13 and rotavirus, both due at 2 months.
key_concept:
Saudi infant schedule.
  • Birth: BCG, HepB
  • 2 and 4 months: IPV, DTaP, HepB, Hib, PCV13, Rota
  • 6 months: OPV, IPV, DTaP, HepB, Hib, PCV13 (no rota)
  • 9 months: measles, MCV4
  • 12 months: OPV, MMR, PCV13, MCV4
  • 18 months: OPV, DTaP, Hib, MMR, varicella, HepA
exam_pearl: Rotavirus is only at 2 and 4 months; MMR and HepA never appear before 12 months.

stem: A 1-year-old infant presents to the Vaccination Clinic with a normal exam and growth. What are the recommended vaccines according to the national program?
why_right: This recall's key is OPV, MMR, varicella and PCV, following a schedule version that gave varicella at 12 months. At the 1-year visit OPV, MMR and PCV are all due, and C is the option with the most correct 12-month vaccines and nothing from the infant series or the 18-month visit.
why_wrong_block:
A. OPV, MMR, HAV, PCV: hepatitis A is given at 18 and 24 months, not at 12 months.
B. Varicella, PCV, HIB: Hib is given at 2, 4, 6 and 18 months, not 12, and OPV and MMR, which are due at 12 months, are missing.
D. OPV, MMR, varicella: omits the PCV13 booster, which is due at 12 months.
key_concept:
12-month Saudi visit: OPV, MMR, PCV13, MCV4.
  • 9 months: measles, MCV4
  • 12 months: OPV, MMR, PCV13, MCV4
  • 18 months: OPV, DTaP, Hib, MMR, varicella, HepA
  • 24 months: HepA second dose
  • School entry: OPV, DTaP, MMR, varicella
exam_pearl: If an option reads OPV, MMR, MCV4, PCV, that is the current 12-month set; varicella and HepA belong to 18 months.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Other version (Saudi national program): A. OPV. MMR, HAV, PCV; B. Varicella, PCV, HIB; C. OPV, MMR, MCV4, PCV; D. OPV, MMR, varicella, DTP; 'Answer: C'.
Other marked answers: Other recall version, Answer line: C. OPV, MMR, MCV4, PCV

stem: 6-Year-Old Pre-School Screening Vaccines (Saudi Program)
why_right: At pre-school (primary school entry) the Saudi national program gives four boosters: OPV, DTaP, MMR and varicella. Option C lists exactly this set, so it is the school entry visit.
why_wrong_block:
A. MMR, DTP and OPV are all given at school entry, but the list is incomplete because the varicella booster is missing.
B. Hepatitis B is finished in infancy (birth, 2, 4, 6 months) and hepatitis A is given at 18 and 24 months, so neither belongs to the school entry visit.
D. PCV is an infant vaccine (2, 4, 6 and 12 months); it is not repeated at school entry, where DTaP should be in its place.
key_concept:
Saudi schedule: know each visit's set.
  • Birth: BCG + HBV
  • 2 and 4 mo: IPV, DTaP, HBV, Hib, PCV, Rotavirus
  • 6 mo: OPV, IPV, DTaP, HBV, Hib, PCV (no rotavirus)
  • 9 mo: Measles + MCV4; 12 mo: OPV, MMR, PCV, MCV4
  • 18 mo: OPV, DTaP, Hib, MMR, Varicella, HAV; 24 mo: HAV
  • School entry: OPV, DTaP, MMR, Varicella
exam_pearl: Any option with HBV, HAV, Hib or PCV is an infant or toddler visit, not school entry.

stem: A 10-year-old boy fell from a tree and hit his head. He had a brief loss of consciousness followed by a seizure for one minute which resolved completely. Upon arrival to the ER, he is in a post-ictal state but arousable. he is conscious, oriented, and Pupils are equal and reactive. No focal neurological deficit. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptC: Observe in the ER for 2 hours
why_right: This child had loss of consciousness and then a post-traumatic seizure, and he is still post-ictal, which counts as altered mental status. Altered mental status after head trauma is a high-risk feature that mandates an urgent non-contrast CT head, and an impact seizure itself is an indication for imaging to exclude intracranial bleeding. Non-contrast CT is fast and shows acute blood and fractures best.
why_wrong_block:
B. Admission for observation fits a child with only intermediate-risk features (brief LOC, vomiting, headache) and a normal mental status; with a seizure and post-ictal state, imaging must come first.
C. A short ER observation is an option only for intermediate-risk children with normal mental status; it would delay diagnosis of a bleed in a child who seized.
D. Discharge is only for a child with none of the risk features (no LOC, no vomiting, normal mental status); this child had LOC and a seizure.
key_concept:
PECARN, child ≥2 years:
  • CT now: altered mental status, GCS <15, signs of basilar skull fracture
  • Observation vs CT: history of LOC, vomiting, severe headache, severe mechanism
  • No CT, discharge: none of the above
  • Post-traumatic seizure or post-ictal state = treat as high risk, image
  • Imaging of choice in acute head trauma: non-contrast CT
exam_pearl: Brief LOC alone = observe or CT; LOC plus seizure / post-ictal = urgent CT.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Short version: Young boy fell and hit his head; seizure for one minute resolved completely; conscious, oriented, no neurological deficit. Options: Urgent non-contrast CT (highlighted) / Admission and observe for 24 hours / Discharge.

stem: Girl was playing in the garden and fall down then she LOC and start do vomit then become stable and present to ER What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: This recall's key is neuro consultation because the girl had two features suggesting possible brain injury after a fall: loss of consciousness and vomiting. The source treats these as red flags that need specialist neurological assessment (with imaging) before she can be sent home, even though she is now stable.
why_wrong_block:
B. Under this key, LOC plus vomiting after a fall needs specialist assessment rather than passive waiting; also, a fixed 24 h admission is longer than the few hours of ER observation usually used for intermediate-risk children.
C. Discharge is only for a child with no LOC, no vomiting, no severe headache and a normal mental status; this girl had both LOC and vomiting.
key_concept:
Minor head trauma in children (PECARN):
  • Altered mental status, GCS <15, skull fracture signs: CT head
  • LOC, vomiting, severe headache, severe mechanism: observation vs CT
  • None: discharge with head injury advice
  • Neurosurgery is involved when CT shows a lesion or the child deteriorates
exam_pearl: LOC or vomiting after a fall rules out simple discharge; the exam then asks you to pick between observation, CT and referral.

stem: Year Old Child Presents With 2 Months History Of Epigastric Pain That Wakes Him Up At Night, Mother Mentioned A History Of PUD, What Is The Confirmatory Test?
highlight_terms_source: Epigastric Pain That Wakes Him Up At Night
why_right: Two months of epigastric pain that wakes him at night with a family history of PUD suggests peptic ulcer disease, often with H. pylori. The lead-in asks for the confirmatory test: only upper GI endoscopy shows the ulcer directly, and biopsy confirms H. pylori and excludes other pathology. Noninvasive tests can suggest H. pylori but cannot confirm an ulcer.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC: may show anemia from chronic blood loss, but it is nonspecific and cannot confirm an ulcer.
B. Abdominal ultrasound: useful for gallstones, pancreatic or hepatic disease, but it cannot see the gastric or duodenal mucosa.
D. H. pylori stool antigen only: detects infection and is mainly used to confirm eradication after treatment; it cannot show an ulcer, and in children diagnosis should be by endoscopy with biopsy rather than a noninvasive test alone.
key_concept:
Suspected PUD in a child:
  • Clues: epigastric pain waking at night, family history, hematemesis or melena
  • Confirm: upper GI endoscopy with biopsy (ulcer + H. pylori histology/culture)
  • Noninvasive tests (urea breath test, stool antigen): mainly to confirm eradication; not for initial diagnosis in children
  • Treat H. pylori: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin; quadruple therapy if failed
exam_pearl: "Confirmatory" for PUD = endoscopy with biopsy; urea breath test or stool antigen are the answer when the question asks how to confirm eradication.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0294).

stem: A 3-Month-Old Infant With Noisy Breath Since Birth Changes With Positioning, Disappears In Prone Position And Becomes More Obvious With Supine Position. Examination And Growth Are Normal. What Counseling Should Be Given?
why_right: Noisy breathing since birth that disappears prone and is worse supine, with normal growth, is laryngomalacia. It is self-limiting and usually resolves by 1 to 2 years, so the mother is reassured that it will improve by the first birthday.
why_wrong_block:
A. Laryngomalacia may peak in the first months but it does not progressively worsen; it settles as the airway cartilage matures.
B. Surgery (supraglottoplasty) is only for severe cases with failure to thrive, apnoea, cyanosis or feeding difficulty; this infant is growing normally.
C. It is not a normal sound; it is a real but benign floppy larynx (laryngomalacia), and calling it normal would miss the need for follow-up and warning signs.
key_concept:
Positional noisy breathing in infants:
  • Laryngomalacia: inspiratory stridor, disappears prone, worse supine; diagnosed by laryngoscopy
  • Tracheomalacia: disappears supine; diagnosed by bronchoscopy
  • Both self-limiting, resolve by 1 to 2 years
  • Surgery only with failure to thrive, apnoea, cyanosis, feeding problems
exam_pearl: Normal growth = reassure; failure to thrive or apnoea = refer for surgery.

stem: 2-Day-Old Infant, 5.2 Kg At Birth, Hypoglycemia, Mother Had Gestational Diabetes Treated With Insulin. Cause Of Hypoglycemia?
why_right: The mother had insulin-treated gestational diabetes and the baby is macrosomic (5.2 kg). Maternal hyperglycaemia crosses the placenta and drives fetal beta-cell hyperplasia; after the cord is cut the glucose supply stops but the infant's hyperinsulinaemia continues, causing neonatal hypoglycaemia in the first days.
why_wrong_block:
A. Organic acidaemias present after feeding starts with vomiting, lethargy and metabolic acidosis with ketosis; nothing here suggests an inborn error, and the maternal diabetes explains the picture.
C. Adrenal insufficiency (e.g. congenital adrenal hyperplasia) gives hypoglycaemia with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, shock or ambiguous genitalia, not macrosomia in an infant of a diabetic mother.
D. Isolated glucagon deficiency is a very rare cause of neonatal hypoglycaemia and has no link to maternal diabetes or macrosomia.
key_concept:
Infant of diabetic mother (IDM):
  • Mechanism: maternal glucose → fetal hyperglycaemia → beta-cell hyperplasia → hyperinsulinaemia
  • Macrosomia → shoulder dystocia, Erb palsy
  • Neonatal hypoglycaemia in the first hours to days
  • Also: hypocalcaemia, polycythaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia, RDS, cardiomyopathy
exam_pearl: Large baby + diabetic mother + low glucose = hyperinsulinism, not an enzyme or hormone deficiency.

stem: Elderly patient in 70s Hx of HTN, brought by his son. He stated to forget recent events but remembers old events. He forgets names. He misplaced his items and can't find them, social activities withdrawal due to lack of interest. Mini Mental exam was done and the result was low (i can't remember exactly the number) On MRI: There was cortical atrophy What medication to start?
highlight_terms_source: forget recent events but remembers old events
why_right: An elderly man with recent memory loss but preserved remote memory, forgetting names, misplacing items, withdrawal, a low MMSE and cortical atrophy on MRI has Alzheimer disease. The lead-in asks which medication to start, and first-line drug therapy for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease is a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine), which modestly improves or stabilises cognition and function.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antipsychotics do not treat the cognitive deficit and raise mortality in elderly patients with dementia; they are reserved for severe psychosis or agitation that endangers the patient or others.
B. His withdrawal reflects apathy from dementia, not a depressive episode; an antidepressant is right when there are core depressive features (low mood, guilt) or pseudodementia, not progressive amnestic decline with atrophy.
key_concept:
Alzheimer disease: recent memory lost first, remote memory kept, progressive decline; treat with a cholinesterase inhibitor.
  • Mild to moderate: donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine
  • Moderate to severe: add or use memantine (NMDA antagonist)
  • Imaging first to exclude structural causes; Alzheimer shows cortical and hippocampal atrophy
  • Benign forgetfulness: does not impair daily function
  • Antipsychotics only for dangerous psychosis or agitation
exam_pearl: Social withdrawal in dementia is usually apathy; do not let it pull you toward an antidepressant when the picture is amnestic decline with atrophy.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0282).

stem: 6-week-old infant presents with projectile vomiting after feeds, poor weight gain, and dehydration. Ultrasound shows pyloric thickening. What is the initial management?
OptC: IV fluids and prepare for pyloromyotomy
why_right: A 6-week-old with projectile vomiting, poor weight gain and pyloric thickening on ultrasound has pyloric stenosis, already confirmed. Because he is dehydrated (and usually has hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis), the first step is IV fluid and electrolyte correction, then pyloromyotomy once he is stable. The lead-in asks for initial management, which is why fluids come before the operation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Barium study was used before ultrasound; the diagnosis is already made on ultrasound, so further imaging adds nothing.
B. Changing feeds treats reflux or milk intolerance; pyloric stenosis is a mechanical obstruction that needs surgery.
D. Reassurance fits physiological reflux (happy spitter, normal weight gain); this baby is dehydrated and failing to gain weight.
key_concept:
Pyloric stenosis:
  • Age 2 to 8 weeks, first-born, non-bilious projectile vomiting, hungry after vomiting
  • Olive-like mass in epigastrium / RUQ
  • Labs: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Investigation: abdominal ultrasound (X-ray: single bubble)
  • Management: correct fluids and electrolytes first, then pyloromyotomy
exam_pearl: "Initial" = IV fluids and electrolytes; "definitive / most appropriate" = pyloromyotomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other versions: screenshot of 5-month-old with non-bilious vomiting, dehydration, olive-shaped epigastric mass, 'most appropriate management' marked **A. Pyloromyotomy (vs Balloon dilatation, Gastrojejunostomy). Q: Pedia boy with non-bilious projectile vomiting and epigastric mass, Mx? A-Pylorotomy.

stem: Pediatric came after a fall while playing, currently stable. ECG picture provided and was SVT. What is the treatment (not sure if it initial or most appropriate) ?
why_right: The ECG shows SVT and the child is stable. For stable narrow-complex SVT, vagal manoeuvres come first (ice to the face in children, Valsalva); since they are not offered, IV adenosine as a rapid bolus is the drug of choice. It transiently blocks the AV node, terminating re-entry and also clarifying the rhythm.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amiodarone is for SVT refractory to adenosine or for wide-complex tachycardia, usually with expert input; it is not first line.
C. Synchronised cardioversion is for unstable SVT (hypotension, poor perfusion, altered consciousness); this child is stable.
D. Beta blockers are used for prevention of recurrences or as later options, not to terminate an acute episode first.
key_concept:
SVT algorithm (PALS / adult similar):
  • Step 1: stable or unstable?
  • Unstable: synchronised cardioversion
  • Stable: vagal manoeuvres (ice to face in infants and children, Valsalva)
  • Then IV adenosine, rapid push with flush, repeat at higher dose
  • Refractory: specialist drugs (e.g. amiodarone) or cardioversion
exam_pearl: The word that flips the answer is STABLE vs UNSTABLE: stable = adenosine, unstable = cardioversion (a duplicate of this recall is keyed to cardioversion).
compiler_note:
⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0360 → C. Cardioversion. Confirm before the exam.
Compiler note: Short version: picture provided and was SVT, treatment? A. Amiodarone, B. Adenosine if Stable, C. Cardioversion if Unstable. Keyword is STABLE SVT: stable = adenosine, unstable = synchronized cardioversion. Amiodarone for refractory/wide-complex, not first line; cardioversion reserved for unstable; beta blocker for prevention/second line. Algorithm: first vagal maneuvers (Valsalva, ice to face in children); if not listed, IV adenosine rapid bolus ✅ (blocks AV node, diagnostic + therapeutic, drug of choice for stable narrow-complex SVT). Ref: AHA PALS 2020.

stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with cough, nasal congestion, fever, and difficulty breathing for 2 days (typical bronchiolitis). On examination, he has tachypnea, respiratory retractions. His oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptA: Reassure and discharge home with nasal saline drops
OptB: Admit for observation, respiratory monitoring, oxygen, and hydration & Suctioning
why_right: A 6-month-old with coryza, cough and fever followed by tachypnoea and retractions has bronchiolitis. His SpO2 is 88% on room air with increased work of breathing, so he needs admission for supportive care: oxygen, hydration, nasal suctioning and monitoring.
why_wrong_block: A. Home care with saline drops fits mild bronchiolitis with good saturation and adequate feeding; hypoxia and retractions make discharge unsafe.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis (usually RSV):
  • URTI symptoms then LRTI signs (wheeze, crackles, tachypnoea, retractions) in an infant
  • Clinical diagnosis; CXR not routine
  • Treatment is supportive: oxygen, hydration, nasal suction
  • Admit: hypoxia, marked distress, apnoea, poor feeding or dehydration
  • Bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely used
exam_pearl: Low saturation + retractions = admit for oxygen; normal saturation and feeding well = home.

stem: 13-year-old obese boy presents with persistent hypertension documented on multiple visits. Examination reveals acanthosis nigricans over the neck and axillae. Patient also has [headache sweating and palpitations] What is the next step to establish diagnosis?
why_right: Persistent hypertension with the classic triad of headache, sweating and palpitations points to pheochromocytoma (a catecholamine-secreting tumour). The step that establishes the diagnosis is biochemical: measure catecholamines and their metabolites (plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary catecholamines/metanephrines). The obesity and acanthosis nigricans reflect insulin resistance and are a distractor here.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cortisol and ACTH test for Cushing syndrome, suggested by purple striae, central obesity, short stature or growth failure; the adrenergic triad points elsewhere.
C. Renal ultrasound looks for renal parenchymal or renovascular causes, the commonest secondary causes in young children, but it does not explain episodic sweating and palpitations.
D. Ambulatory BP monitoring confirms true hypertension (excludes white coat effect); here hypertension is already documented on multiple visits and the question asks for the cause.
key_concept:
Secondary hypertension clues in children:
  • Headache + sweating + palpitations: pheochromocytoma → plasma free metanephrines / urinary catecholamines
  • Striae, central obesity, growth failure: Cushing → cortisol tests
  • Young child, abnormal urine, bruit: renal → renal US / Doppler
  • Obese adolescent with acanthosis and no other clues: primary (obesity-related) HTN
exam_pearl: Without the adrenergic triad, an obese teen with acanthosis and high BP is usually primary hypertension; the triad is what makes it catecholamines.
compiler_note: Compiler note: AboSarah: most likely diagnosis pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting tumor causing episodic or persistent hypertension). Obese with acanthosis nigricans = insulin resistance. Triad headache + sweating + palpitations = pheochromocytoma until proven otherwise. Next step: measure catecholamines or metanephrines (plasma free metanephrines best screening; or 24-hour urinary catecholamines/metanephrines). HTN + episodic adrenergic symptoms in a child/adolescent: check catecholamines first.

stem: 6-Year-Old Complaining Of Bedwetting. He Has Never Been Dry At Night. His Brother Had The Same Problem What's Next Step?
why_right: A 6-year-old who has never been dry at night has primary nocturnal enuresis, and a sibling with the same problem shows the strong familial tendency. At this age bedwetting is still common and resolves spontaneously in most children each year, so the first step is reassurance with simple behavioural advice (no punishment, voiding before bed, limiting evening fluids).
why_wrong_block:
B. Desmopressin is for older children when behavioural measures and the alarm fail, or for short-term needs such as sleepovers; it is not the first step at 6.
C. Toilet training addresses daytime continence, which is usually already achieved; nighttime dryness depends on bladder maturation and ADH rhythm, not training.
D. The enuresis alarm is the most effective active treatment once a motivated older child and family want treatment after behavioural measures; it is not the first step here.
key_concept:
Primary nocturnal enuresis:
  • Bedwetting is considered significant after about 6 years
  • Strong family history; spontaneous resolution each year
  • Ladder: reassurance and behavioural measures → enuresis alarm → desmopressin (oral, not intranasal)
  • Secondary enuresis (previously dry) or daytime symptoms: look for UTI, diabetes, constipation, stress
exam_pearl: Never dry + family history + young age = reassure; new bedwetting after being dry = investigate (urinalysis, glucose).
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0341).

stem: 10 years old boy presented to the emergency department with fever, headache and sore throat for 2 days, in examination there were enlarged tonsils with exudate and pharyngeal petechiae. He had enlargement of anterior and posterior cervical lymph nodes. The rapid strep test was negative. BP: 100/65 T: 39 Others normal. What's the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: enlarged tonsils with exudate and pharyngeal petechiae
why_right: The picture is classic for group A strep pharyngitis: "fever 39", "tonsils with exudate", "pharyngeal petechiae" and enlarged cervical nodes in a 10 year old. The rapid strep test has high specificity but imperfect sensitivity, so in a child a negative rapid test must be backed up by a throat culture before GAS is excluded. Missing GAS in a child matters because untreated infection carries the risk of acute rheumatic fever.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral penicillin V is the treatment once GAS is confirmed (positive rapid test or positive culture); starting it on clinical suspicion after a negative rapid test, without culture, is not the recommended pathway.
C. Reassurance would fit a mild viral picture once GAS is excluded; with high fever, exudate and petechiae, a negative rapid test alone cannot rule out strep in a child.
D. This option is missing from the recall, so it cannot be the keyed answer.
key_concept:
Suspected GAS pharyngitis: rapid antigen test first, culture to confirm a negative result in children.
  • Rapid test positive: treat (penicillin V or amoxicillin, 10 days)
  • Rapid test negative, child or adolescent: throat culture
  • Rapid test negative, adult: no culture needed
  • Antibiotics only after GAS is confirmed
  • Goal of treatment in children: prevent acute rheumatic fever
exam_pearl: Negative rapid strep in a child = send a culture; in an adult = stop there. Watch for a lead-in that says "rapid test positive", which flips the answer to penicillin.
compiler_note:
⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-1987 → A. Oral penicillin V. Confirm before the exam.
Compiler note: Strong clinical features of GAS pharyngitis (fever 39, sore throat, tonsillar exudates, pharyngeal petechiae, cervical lymphadenopathy). However RADT is negative; in children and adolescents a negative rapid strep test MUST be confirmed with throat culture (RADT specificity high, sensitivity imperfect, false negatives occur; must not miss GAS due to rheumatic fever risk). Child (<18 yrs): throat culture; adult: no culture needed. Treatment after confirmation: oral penicillin V for 10 days (or amoxicillin). Penicillin allergy: cephalexin (non-anaphylactic), azithromycin or clindamycin (true anaphylaxis). Treatment prevents acute rheumatic fever. Refs: IDSA, AAP, CDC.

stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because her mother had felt a mass in the abdomen last night when she was bathing her. She has been otherwise well with no weight loss, fever, or bone pain. Her blood pressure is 130/80 mmH. Physical examination shows a well-thriving kid with a palpable firm mass in the right flank (see lab results). Color Clear clear or light yellow, pH 7.0 4.3-8 Specific gravity 1010 1001-1030. Protein Absent. Glucose Absent. Ketones Absent. Nitrite Absent. Hemoglobin ++. Leukocytes Absent 0-3 per high power field. Erythrocytes 50 0-2 per high power field. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her diagnostic work-up?
OptD: Plain abdominal radiography and abdominal ultrasonography
why_right: A well 4 year old with a firm "right flank mass", microscopic hematuria (erythrocytes 50/HPF) and raised BP (130/80), with no fever, weight loss or bone pain, is suspicious for Wilms tumor. The first diagnostic step for a pediatric abdominal mass is ultrasound with a plain film: ultrasound shows the organ of origin, solid vs cystic nature, renal vein or IVC extension and the other kidney, while the plain film looks for calcification. CT or MRI comes afterwards for staging.
why_wrong_block:
A. A plain film alone cannot define the organ of origin or the extent of the mass; it is only an adjunct (calcification favors neuroblastoma).
B. CT is used after ultrasound for staging (and chest CT for lung metastases); it is not the first step and adds radiation.
C. MRI is a later staging study that often needs sedation in a young child; ultrasound comes first.
key_concept:
Pediatric abdominal mass: start cheap and radiation free, then stage.
  • Step 1: abdominal ultrasound (plus plain film)
  • Step 2: CT or MRI abdomen for staging
  • Wilms clues: well child, flank mass, hematuria, hypertension
  • Neuroblastoma clues: unwell child, crosses midline, calcification, bone pain
exam_pearl: "Next step" for a child's flank mass is ultrasound, not CT; CT is the answer only when the lead-in asks about staging.

stem: A 26-year-old woman complains of marked fear whenever dealing with unfamiliar people, as she is afraid of embarrassment. She was referred to a local psychologist for assessment and management. Which of the following will benefit from cognitive behavioral therapy?
highlight_terms_source: marked fear whenever dealing with unfamiliar people
why_right: Marked fear when dealing with unfamiliar people because she is afraid of embarrassment is social phobia (social anxiety disorder). Anxiety disorders are the classic condition where CBT is the first line treatment, using cognitive restructuring and graded exposure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Schizophrenia: treated mainly with antipsychotics; CBT is only an adjunct, and the stem shows no psychotic features.
C. Postpartum psychosis: a psychiatric emergency needing admission and antipsychotics (or ECT), not CBT; she is not postpartum.
D. Depression with hallucination: psychotic depression needs an antidepressant plus antipsychotic or ECT; CBT alone is not appropriate.
key_concept:
CBT is first line where there is no psychosis.
  • Social phobia: fear of scrutiny or embarrassment; CBT, SSRI if needed.
  • Panic disorder, GAD, OCD, phobias: CBT.
  • Psychotic disorders: antipsychotics first; CBT only adjunct.
exam_pearl: Any option containing psychosis or hallucinations is a drug (or ECT) answer, not a CBT answer.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with a 2-day history of fever and painful skin eruption over the left side of his chest. His physical examination reveals a skin eruption consisting of maculopapular lesions and vesicles with some skin crusting over the left side of his chest. His systemic examinations are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate action to confirm the diagnosis?
OptC: Swab from skin lesion for culture
highlight_terms_source: painful skin eruption over the left side of his chest
maculopapular lesions and vesicles with some skin crusting
why_right: A "painful skin eruption over the left side of his chest" with "maculopapular lesions and vesicles" and "crusting" is a unilateral dermatomal rash, the textbook picture of herpes zoster (shingles). Shingles is a clinical diagnosis, so in a typical presentation in a systemically well patient no investigation is needed to confirm it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skin biopsy is invasive and unnecessary for a typical dermatomal zoster rash; it is used for atypical lesions or suspected malignancy.
B. Zoster is VZV reactivation; blood cultures detect bacteria and have no role in a systemically well patient.
C. Viral culture is slow and insensitive and not required here; lesion swab for PCR is reserved for atypical or disseminated cases or immunocompromised patients.
key_concept:
Herpes zoster: dermatomal, unilateral, painful vesicular rash = clinical diagnosis.
  • Prodrome: pain or burning before the rash
  • Does not cross the midline
  • Typical case: no tests
  • Atypical or immunocompromised: vesicle swab PCR
  • Treat with oral antiviral (acyclovir, valacyclovir) early
exam_pearl: Unilateral band-like vesicular rash that stops at the midline = shingles; the answer is "no investigation" unless the picture is atypical.

stem: There was a patient with a clinical scenario of Alzheimer's disease prescribed donepezil, but no improvement was noticed for 6 months. MRI showing cortical atrophy. How should his medications be adjusted?
highlight_terms_source: no improvement was noticed for 6 months
why_right: This recall's key is switching donepezil to memantine: the patient with Alzheimer disease has had no improvement after 6 months of donepezil, and MRI shows cortical atrophy (established, progressing disease). The source's reasoning is that the cholinesterase inhibitor has failed, so treatment moves to the other drug class, the NMDA antagonist memantine, which is used in moderate to severe disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Add sertraline: treats coexisting depression or anxiety in dementia; the stem gives no mood symptoms and it does not treat cognition.
B. Add memantine: combination therapy is used when disease progresses to moderate or severe stage while the cholinesterase inhibitor is still tolerated; this recall keys a switch instead.
D. Switch donepezil to rivastigmine: changing to another cholinesterase inhibitor is mainly for intolerance of donepezil; this key treats the problem as class failure and moves to memantine.
key_concept:
Alzheimer drug ladder.
  • Mild to moderate: cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine).
  • Moderate to severe or AChEI not tolerated: memantine.
  • Already on AChEI and progressing to moderate or severe: memantine can be added.
  • Depression in dementia: SSRI such as sertraline.
exam_pearl: Read the options: switch vs add memantine is the fork, and this recall's key is the switch.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): Alzheimer prescribed donepezil for 6 months but no improvement; asking how to adjust his meds (No mention of MMSE drop). Same options; highlighted: C. Change Donepezil To Memantine.

stem: A 24-hour-old neonate with ambiguous genitalia. 17-hydroxyprogesterone was abnormally high (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Sodium 128 134-146 mmol/L Potassium 6.8 3.5-5.1 mmol/L Bicarbonate 16 21-28 mmol/L Glucose 2.5 2.8-5 mmol/L (Newborn) 3.3-5.5 mmol/L (Child). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: "Ambiguous genitalia" with an "abnormally high" 17-hydroxyprogesterone plus salt wasting (Na 128, K 6.8, HCO3 16) and hypoglycemia (2.5) is classic salt-wasting CAH from 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The block stops both cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, so 17-OHP builds up and is diverted to androgens (virilizing a 46,XX baby), aldosterone loss causes salt wasting and cortisol loss causes hypoglycemia. It is by far the most common form of CAH.
why_wrong_block:
B. 17-hydroxylase deficiency causes mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalemia) with undervirilized males and absent puberty, and 17-OHP is low, not high.
C. 11-beta hydroxylase deficiency also virilizes, but 11-deoxycorticosterone excess gives hypertension and hypokalemia, not hyponatremia with hyperkalemia.
D. 3-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency is rare, undervirilizes males and raises DHEA and 17-hydroxypregnenolone rather than a predominant 17-OHP rise.
key_concept:
CAH: match the electrolytes and BP to the enzyme.
  • 21-hydroxylase: high 17-OHP, low Na, high K, virilized female, BP low
  • 11-beta hydroxylase: virilized, hypertension, low K
  • 17-hydroxylase: hypertension, low K, undervirilized male, no puberty
  • 3-beta HSD: salt wasting, undervirilized male, high DHEA
  • All autosomal recessive
exam_pearl: Virilization + HYPERtension = 11-beta hydroxylase; virilization + salt wasting = 21-hydroxylase.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Details: NCBI Bookshelf NBK279168.

stem: A 13-year-old healthy girl is brought by her mother with concerns about not yet starting menstruation. Examination reveals sparse hair covering the labia majora, not extending onto the mons pubis. She has developed breast buds and papilla and areola enlargement, with no separation in contour between the breast and areola. Which Tanner stage would this girl be assigned to?
highlight_terms_source: sparse hair covering the labia majora, not extending onto the mons pubis
no separation in contour between the breast and areola
why_right: "Sparse hair covering the labia majora, not extending onto the mons" is Tanner 2 pubic hair, and "breast buds" with papilla and areolar enlargement is the Tanner 2 breast bud stage. Both axes point to Tanner stage II, so she is in early puberty and amenorrhea at 13 is expected (menarche usually follows later).
why_wrong_block:
A. Tanner I is prepubertal: only the nipple is raised and there is no pubic hair; she already has breast buds and labial hair.
C. Tanner III shows darker, coarser, curlier hair spreading onto the mons with further breast and areolar enlargement; the stem's "no separation in contour" wording echoes stage III breast, but her hair stops at the labia and the breast is still described as buds.
D. Tanner IV shows the areola and nipple forming a secondary mound and adult-type hair over a smaller area than adults.
key_concept:
Female Tanner staging:
  • I: nipple raised only; no pubic hair
  • II: breast bud, areola enlarges; sparse hair along labia
  • III: breast and areola enlarge with no contour separation; coarse hair spreads onto mons
  • IV: areola and nipple form secondary mound; adult hair, smaller area
  • V: mature contour; adult triangle spreading to medial thighs
exam_pearl: Trap: "no separation in contour between breast and areola" is the Tanner III breast phrase, but labia-only hair and breast buds anchor this key to II.

stem: A child presents with symptoms suggestive of bronchial asthma, with episodes that worsen during upper respiratory tract infections. At this visit, the chest X-ray is normal.
