What is the best information to give the parents regarding this case? (almost exactly like this, if anyone in the comments can add please)
OptA: Bronchial asthma increases the risk of upper respiratory tract infections.
OptB: Polyphonic wheeze occurs on exertion (not exercise)
OptC: Between attacks, the chest X-ray is normal.
highlight_terms_source: worsen during upper respiratory tract infections
why_right: This recall's key is C: in childhood asthma the chest X-ray is usually normal between attacks, which fits the stem's "chest X-ray is normal" and is the reassuring, accurate fact to give parents. Asthma is a clinical diagnosis of variable airflow obstruction; imaging is not needed to make it and a normal film does not exclude it. During acute attacks the film may show hyperinflation, but it returns to normal.
why_wrong_block:
A. The relationship runs the other way: viral URTIs are a common trigger of asthma exacerbations, but asthma does not make children catch more URTIs.
B. Polyphonic expiratory wheeze is a genuine asthma feature, typically set off by exercise, cold air or viral infections; the recalled wording is garbled, and C is the cleaner, always true counselling point for parents of a child with a normal film.
D. This option text is not recalled, so it cannot be the keyed answer.
key_concept:
Childhood asthma: clinical diagnosis, normal investigations between episodes.
  • Triggers: viral URTI, exercise, allergens, smoke, cold air
  • Wheeze: polyphonic, expiratory, variable
  • CXR: normal between attacks; hyperinflation during attacks
  • CXR is used to exclude other causes (foreign body, pneumonia), not to diagnose asthma
exam_pearl: URTIs trigger asthma attacks; asthma does not cause URTIs. Don't fall for the reversed causality option.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler note: 'B/C??' (uncertain between B and C).
Other marked answers: Compiler uncertain: B

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the clinic. The mother is concerned that her child is short. She appears to be short. In a systemic review, he is asymptomatic. Physical examination is normal (see lab results and report). Blood pressure 130/85 mmHg, Heart rate 75/min, Respiratory rate 16/min, Temperature 37.2 C, Weight 25 kg, Height 120 cm. Test / Result / Normal: Thyroid stimulating hormone 3.2 (0.4-5.0 U/L); Follicle stimulating hormone 1.4 (1.0-1.6 IU/L); Luteinizing hormone 0.1 (0.05-0.5 IU/L); Growth hormone 4.9 (2-10 pg/L); Free Testosterone 38.2 (10.4-41.6 mol/L); Insulin like growth factor-1 18 (67-405 ng/mL). X-ray of left wrist and hand: The bone age is as a 6-year-old child. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: The bone age is as a 6-year-old child
why_right: The decisive findings are IGF-1 18 (well below the 67-405 range) and a bone age of 6 years at chronological age 9, a 3 year delay. IGF-1 is produced in response to GH, so a low IGF-1 shows inadequate GH action even though the single random GH (4.9) looks normal; random GH is pulsatile and unreliable. A delayed bone age excludes familial short stature, and the low IGF-1 separates GH deficiency from constitutional delay, so growth hormone deficiency is the most likely diagnosis (confirmed later with GH stimulation testing).
why_wrong_block:
A. Failure to thrive is weight faltering from poor intake or illness; this child is asymptomatic with a normal exam and the abnormal result is a low IGF-1.
B. Familial short stature has a normal bone age and normal GH/IGF-1, with short parents; here bone age is delayed 3 years and IGF-1 is low.
D. This option is missing from the recall, so it cannot be the keyed answer. If it was constitutional growth delay: bone age is also delayed, but IGF-1 is normal for bone age and there is a family history of late puberty.
key_concept:
Short stature: use bone age and IGF-1 to split normal variants from disease.
  • Familial: bone age = chronological age, normal velocity, short parents
  • Constitutional delay: bone age delayed, normal IGF-1 for bone age, late puberty in family
  • GH deficiency: bone age delayed, low IGF-1, slow velocity
  • Random GH is unreliable; IGF-1 screens, stimulation test confirms
exam_pearl: A "normal" random GH does not exclude GH deficiency; a low IGF-1 does the talking.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: C, MG.

stem: A 14-month-old boy is brought to the clinic with severe gram-positive bacterial pneumonia, was referred to the hospital by the family physician. This is his third infection in 4 months. He has 2 healthy sisters aged 3 and 5 years. The family lost a boy at 10 months of age to bacterial pneumonia 6 years ago. The family doctor has sent along some blood test results that shows low all classes of serum immunoglobulin levels, few B cells, but normal numbers and functioning of T cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: low all classes of serum immunoglobulin
normal numbers and functioning of T cells
why_right: Two affected boys (this child and a brother who died at 10 months of pneumonia) with "2 healthy sisters" points to X-linked recessive inheritance. "Low all classes" of immunoglobulin with "few B cells" and normal T cells is the hallmark of X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia: a BTK defect stops pro-B cells maturing, so no plasma cells and no antibodies. Onset after about 6 months, as maternal IgG wanes, with recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections, fits this 14 month old.
why_wrong_block:
A. Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy is usually mild with normal B cell numbers and does not cause severe pneumonia or kill a sibling.
B. Common variable immunodeficiency presents in older children or adults, B cells are usually present, and it is not X-linked.
C. A CD40/CD40 ligand defect causes hyper IgM syndrome: IgM is normal or high because class switching fails, so not all classes are low and B cells are present.
key_concept:
Antibody deficiency: count the B cells and look at IgM.
  • XLA (Bruton): all Ig low, B cells absent, boys, after 6 months
  • Hyper IgM (CD40L): IgM normal/high, IgG/IgA low
  • CVID: older onset, B cells present but poor antibodies
  • Transient hypogammaglobulinemia: mild, self-resolving, B cells normal
exam_pearl: Low ALL immunoglobulins + ABSENT B cells + affected brothers = Bruton; if IgM is high, think CD40 ligand.

stem: A 7-year-old boy has had recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract bacterial infections since infancy. On examination, he has eczema and areas of ecchymosis on his skin. His brother and a paternal uncle are similarly affected (see lab results). Hb 108 (112-165 g/L); WBC 6 (4.5-10.5); Platelets count 40 (150-400 x 10^9/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract bacterial infections
why_right: The triad is all here: recurrent bacterial infections "since infancy" (immunodeficiency), "eczema", and thrombocytopenia (platelets 40 with ecchymoses), in a boy with affected male relatives. That is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked recessive WAS gene defect that gives small, few platelets plus combined immune dysfunction. Definitive treatment is stem cell transplantation.
why_wrong_block:
A. SCID presents in early infancy with severe viral and opportunistic infections and failure to thrive, and children rarely reach 7 years untreated; it has no eczema with thrombocytopenia.
B. Bruton agammaglobulinemia is also X-linked with recurrent bacterial infections, but it has no eczema and no thrombocytopenia or bruising.
D. DiGeorge (22q11 deletion) gives hypocalcemia, conotruncal heart defects, thymic hypoplasia and facial dysmorphism, not eczema with low platelets.
key_concept:
Immunodeficiency + something extra = the syndrome.
  • + eczema + low small platelets: Wiskott-Aldrich
  • + hypocalcemia + heart defect: DiGeorge
  • + ataxia + telangiectasia: ataxia telangiectasia
  • Bacterial infections only, absent B cells: Bruton
  • Severe infections from birth, failure to thrive: SCID
exam_pearl: Eczema + bleeding/bruising + infections in a boy = Wiskott-Aldrich; drop the eczema and low platelets and it becomes Bruton.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome: rare X-linked recessive immunodeficiency affecting mostly males; triad of low platelet count (microthrombocytopenia), severe eczema, and recurrent infections. Caused by WAS gene mutations impairing immune cell function and platelet production. Management: antibiotics, immunoglobulin infusions, definitive stem cell transplantation.

stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the Pediatrics Emergency Department with vomiting and lethargy. The parents report a weight loss of 1 kg over the last 2 weeks. There has been little appetite, but a lot of thirst and frequent urination. The child appeared sleepy and irritable. Physical examination confirmed dry mucous membranes and a generally reduced skin tone. After running several exams, the pediatrician started IV treatment with ringer lactate plus added electrolytes and a low-dose insulin infusion (see lab results). pH 7.2 (7.36-7.45); Glucose 20 (3.5-5.5 mmol/L); Urine ketones positive. Which of the following complications should be observed?
why_right: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss, vomiting and lethargy with pH 7.2, glucose 20 and positive ketones is new-onset type 1 diabetes in DKA. Once IV fluids and insulin are running, the complication to watch for is cerebral edema: it is the most serious, life-threatening complication of pediatric DKA, is commoner in young children such as this 4 year old, and usually appears in the first hours of treatment. Watch for headache, falling consciousness, bradycardia and rising BP.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypoglycemia is monitored during insulin infusion (dextrose is added as glucose falls), but it is not the feared complication the question targets.
B. Prerenal kidney impairment can occur from dehydration but usually corrects with fluids; it is not the key complication of DKA treatment.
D. DKA causes metabolic acidosis; treatment corrects the acidosis rather than producing a metabolic alkalosis.
key_concept:
Pediatric DKA: fluids, then insulin, then watch the brain.
  • Diagnosis: hyperglycemia + acidosis + ketosis
  • Most feared complication: cerebral edema (young age, first hours of treatment)
  • Warning signs: headache, drowsiness, bradycardia, hypertension
  • Also monitor: glucose (hypoglycemia) and potassium
exam_pearl: In a child on DKA treatment who becomes drowsy or bradycardic, think cerebral edema first, not hypoglycemia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: New-onset Type 1 DM presenting with DKA. In pediatric DKA, cerebral edema is the most serious and life-threatening complication; more common in children <5 years; usually occurs within the first 4-12 hours of treatment; associated with rapid fluid shifts and osmotic changes.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with the complaints of mild abdominal pain, constipation and aggression. The mother told the physician that he is used to eating tissue paper and chipped off wall paint (see lab results and report). RBC 3.9 (4.6-4.8 x 10^12/L); Hb 74 (112-165 g/L); MCH 23 (28-33 pg/cell); MCV 70 (80-95 fl). Peripheral blood smear: Microcytic hypochromic. Which of the following is the most likely type of anaemia?
highlight_terms_source: eating tissue paper and chipped off wall paint
why_right: Pica ("eating tissue paper and chipped off wall paint") with Hb 74, MCV 70, low MCH and a "microcytic hypochromic" smear points to iron deficiency anemia, the commonest microcytic anemia in children. Pica is both a symptom of and a clue to iron deficiency. Eating paint with abdominal pain, constipation and aggression should also prompt a blood lead level, since lead poisoning can coexist and also causes microcytosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aplastic anemia is normocytic with pancytopenia and low reticulocytes, not an isolated microcytic hypochromic anemia.
B. Pernicious anemia (B12 deficiency) is macrocytic with a high MCV; here MCV is 70.
C. Hemolytic anemia is usually normocytic with high reticulocytes, jaundice and raised bilirubin; pica with microcytosis points to iron deficiency.
key_concept:
Classify anemia by MCV first.
  • Microcytic (MCV < 80): iron deficiency, thalassemia trait, lead, chronic disease
  • Normocytic: hemolysis, aplasia, acute blood loss, chronic disease
  • Macrocytic: B12/folate deficiency (pernicious), liver disease
  • Pica + microcytic hypochromic: iron deficiency
exam_pearl: Wall paint + constipation + behavior change = also check lead; but "type of anemia" with low MCV and pica is iron deficiency.

stem: A 9-year-old child presents to Emergency Department with hypovolemic shock. Parents gave history of recent brain surgery and the child has polyuria and increased thirst since then (see lab results). Blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, Heart rate 136/min, Respiratory rate 18/min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 95%. Labs: ABG HCO3- 20, PCO2 35, pH 7.37, PO2 88, Base excess -6, Sodium 177, Potassium 4, Chloride 140, Bicarbonate 20, BUN 8, Creatinine 60, Glucose 4.5. Urine: colorless, clear, Specific gravity 1003, ketones absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
OptD: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
why_right: Polyuria and thirst starting after "recent brain surgery", now with hypovolemic shock, severe hypernatremia (Na 177) and very dilute, "colorless" urine (SG 1003) is central diabetes insipidus from loss of ADH. The kidneys keep losing free water despite dehydration, so serum sodium climbs while urine stays dilute. Normal glucose, absent ketones and near normal pH exclude the other options.
why_wrong_block:
A. DKA needs hyperglycemia, ketosis and acidosis; here glucose is 4.5, ketones are absent and pH is 7.37.
C. Renal tubular acidosis gives a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis; here pH is near normal and the dominant problem is hypernatremia with dilute urine after neurosurgery.
D. SIADH is the mirror image: hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine in a euvolemic patient, not Na 177 with dilute urine and shock.
key_concept:
Sodium and urine concentration separate DI from SIADH.
  • DI: high Na, high serum osmolality, dilute urine (low SG), polyuria
  • SIADH: low Na, low serum osmolality, concentrated urine
  • Central DI causes: neurosurgery, head trauma, pituitary tumors
  • Treatment of central DI: desmopressin
exam_pearl: Post brain surgery: high sodium + dilute urine = DI; low sodium + concentrated urine = SIADH.

stem: A newborn presents with poor feeding, tongue fasciculations, and decreased deep tendon reflexes. What would you tell the parents?
OptA: The condition is mild and will resolve on its own.
OptB: A muscle biopsy is needed to choose the proper treatment.
OptC: With good nutrition, life expectancy can increase.
OptD: There is a new therapy that is more effective if started early.
why_right: A newborn with "poor feeding", "tongue fasciculations" and "decreased deep tendon reflexes" is a floppy infant with a lower motor neuron picture: spinal muscular atrophy type 1 (SMN1 deletion). Disease-modifying therapies (nusinersen, onasemnogene abeparvovec, risdiplam) now exist, and they work best when started early, ideally before major motor neuron loss. So the honest counseling is that effective treatment is available and timing matters.
why_wrong_block:
A. SMA type 1 is severe and progressive; without treatment it causes respiratory failure in infancy. False reassurance is wrong; reassurance fits benign conditions only.
B. Diagnosis is by SMN1 genetic testing, not muscle biopsy, and treatment choice does not depend on biopsy. Biopsy is reserved for suspected primary myopathy with negative genetics.
C. Nutrition and respiratory support are supportive care, but they do not change the natural history the way SMN-targeted therapy does. This statement misses the key message of early disease-modifying treatment.
key_concept:
Floppy infant + tongue fasciculations + absent/low reflexes = SMA (anterior horn cell disease).
  • Cause: homozygous SMN1 deletion; SMN2 copy number modifies severity
  • Type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann): onset before 6 months, never sits
  • Diagnosis: SMN1 genetic test (EMG shows denervation; CK normal or mildly high)
  • Treatment: nusinersen (intrathecal), onasemnogene (gene therapy), risdiplam (oral)
  • Earlier start (even presymptomatic via newborn screening) = better motor outcome
exam_pearl: Fasciculations + areflexia point to the anterior horn cell (SMA); a floppy baby with normal reflexes and alertness issues points to a central cause instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Case of Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), especially Type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann disease): newborn, poor feeding, tongue fasciculations, decreased DTRs, hypotonia; caused by SMN1 gene mutation. There are now disease-modifying therapies (nusinersen, onasemnogene abeparvovec, risdiplam), and outcomes are significantly better when started early (even pre-symptomatic). Correct answer: D. Tongue fasciculations in a floppy baby = think SMA.

stem: 38 weeks with absent deep tendon reflex, tongue fasciculation. EMG showed denervation. Family concerned about the child's condition. What is the appropriate counseling?
OptB: Medication improves symptoms and quality of life
OptC: Medicine is developing and there are new and better options now
highlight_terms_source: absent deep tendon reflex, tongue fasciculation
why_right: "Absent deep tendon reflex", "tongue fasciculation" and EMG "denervation" in a newborn indicate spinal muscular atrophy. This recall's key is that medication improves symptoms and quality of life: SMN-targeted drugs (nusinersen, risdiplam, gene therapy) improve motor function and survival, so the family should be counseled that treatment helps rather than falsely reassured.
why_wrong_block:
A. SMA does not disappear; type 1 is progressive and fatal without treatment. Reassurance is correct only for benign, self-limiting conditions.
C. The statement is true in general, but it is vague and does not tell the family what treatment will do for their child. The keyed option states the concrete benefit (better symptoms and quality of life).
key_concept:
Neonatal hypotonia + areflexia + tongue fasciculations + EMG denervation = SMA.
  • Lower motor neuron lesion at the anterior horn cell
  • Confirm with SMN1 genetic testing
  • Counsel: disease-modifying therapy exists and improves function and survival
  • Best results when started early
  • Plus multidisciplinary supportive care (respiratory, nutrition, physiotherapy)
exam_pearl: In SMA counseling questions, never pick reassurance; choose the option saying treatment exists and helps (especially early).

stem: gravida 41weeks child deliver via NVD and had respiratory distress but not saturated what next?
why_right: A 41-week (late-term) newborn with respiratory distress who is not saturating is hypoxaemic, and the immediate step is supplemental oxygen titrated to target saturation while the cause (meconium aspiration is a concern at this gestation, or TTN) is worked out. Treat the hypoxia first, then investigate and escalate support if oxygen alone fails.
why_wrong_block:
B. Keeping the baby NPO is a reasonable supportive measure in a tachypnoeic neonate to reduce aspiration risk, but it does nothing for the low saturation and is not the next step.
C. Surfactant is for surfactant-deficient RDS in a preterm infant (and sometimes for severe meconium aspiration after intubation); it is not first-line for a term or post-term baby who has only just been started on support.
D. Magnesium sulfate is a maternal drug for preeclampsia/eclampsia and fetal neuroprotection; it has no role as the next step in a hypoxic newborn.
key_concept:
Neonatal respiratory distress with low saturation: oxygen first, then find the cause.
  • Preterm: RDS (surfactant deficiency), may need CPAP and surfactant
  • Term CS: TTN, self-resolving, supportive oxygen
  • Post-term, meconium-stained liquor: meconium aspiration syndrome
  • Escalate oxygen to CPAP/ventilation if saturation does not improve
exam_pearl: Surfactant is the trap: it belongs to the preterm RDS story, not to a 41-week baby whose first need is oxygen.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1520).
Compiler note: A. 30-40% oxygen: first-line management is supplemental oxygen for hypoxia. C. Surfactant: used mainly in preterm RDS, not a 41-week baby. D. Magnesium is not used for neonatal respiratory distress.

stem: Child contact with his maid she had TB, the child +ve igra +ve x ray but no Clinical findings. What should treatment for child? (Picture of lung TB)
highlight_terms_source: contact with his maid she had TB
why_right: The child has a TB contact, a "+ve IGRA" and a "+ve x ray" (picture of lung TB). An abnormal chest X-ray means active pulmonary TB, even without symptoms, so the child needs full anti-TB therapy: rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide (with ethambutol as per local protocol) for the intensive phase, then rifampicin plus isoniazid continuation.
why_wrong_block:
A. 3 months of rifampicin plus isoniazid is a latent TB regimen. It is right only when IGRA is positive and the chest X-ray is normal; here the X-ray is abnormal.
B. 6 months of isoniazid is also a latent TB regimen. Using monotherapy for active disease undertreats it and risks drug resistance.
key_concept:
TB contact + positive IGRA/TST: the chest X-ray decides latent vs active.
  • Normal CXR, no symptoms = latent TB: 6H, 4R or 3HR
  • Abnormal CXR (or symptoms) = active TB: RIPE intensive phase then RI continuation
  • Never treat active TB with 1 or 2 drugs (resistance)
  • Give pyridoxine with isoniazid when indicated
exam_pearl: Same contact, same positive IGRA: abnormal X-ray = RIPE; normal X-ray = latent regimen (compare AS-0245).
compiler_note: Compiler note: IGRA = Interferon-Gamma Release Assay. Positive IGRA + abnormal CXR = active TB disease, so full anti-TB therapy (WHO/pediatric guidelines): Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol (2 months intensive then continuation with RI). IGRA+, CXR normal = latent TB = INH 6 months (or 3HR). Other recall: 9-year-old, household worker with TB, IGRA positive, CXR consolidation: answer Full RIPE therapy.

stem: Child contact with his maid she had TB, the child +ve igra . but no Clinical findings. What should treatment for child? (Picture of Normal CXR)
why_right: A child with a TB contact, "+ve igra", "no Clinical findings" and a "Normal CXR" has latent TB infection. Latent TB is treated with a preventive regimen, and 3 months of rifampicin plus isoniazid (3HR) is one accepted option; shorter rifamycin-based regimens are preferred because adherence is better.
why_wrong_block:
B. Isoniazid for 6 months is also an accepted latent TB regimen, but it is longer with lower completion rates. In this recall the shorter 3HR regimen is keyed as the preferred choice.
C. RIPE is for active TB disease (symptoms or an abnormal chest X-ray). With a normal X-ray and no findings, four drugs are overtreatment.
key_concept:
Positive IGRA + normal CXR + no symptoms = latent TB.
  • Options: isoniazid 6 months, rifampicin 4 months, isoniazid + rifampicin 3 months
  • Shorter rifamycin-based regimens are favoured for adherence
  • Abnormal CXR or symptoms = active TB: RIPE
  • Add pyridoxine with isoniazid when indicated
exam_pearl: When both 6H and 3HR are offered for latent TB, the shorter rifamycin-based regimen is usually the keyed answer; RIPE only if the X-ray is abnormal.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Latent TB (IGRA positive, normal CXR): per 244 note, INH 6 months or 3HR.

stem: A 10 years old DM1 with vomiting/ nausea and lobate breathing, his glucose was 380. pH 7.12. What is the next ?
OptB: IV fluid and regular insulin infusion
why_right: This recall's key is subcutaneous insulin with oral hydration, a regimen that some protocols allow only for mild DKA in an alert child who tolerates oral fluids. However, the stem gives "vomiting/nausea", deep (Kussmaul) breathing, glucose 380 and "pH 7.12", which is moderate DKA in a child who cannot keep oral fluids down. The source itself is split (a screenshot of the same question keys B), so treat this key with caution.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics are given only if there is evidence of infection as the DKA trigger. Nothing in this stem suggests infection.
B. IV fluids followed by a fixed-rate regular insulin infusion is the standard management for moderate to severe DKA with vomiting. In this recall's key it is not the marked answer, but see the concern note.
D. Carbohydrates treat hypoglycemia. This child is hyperglycemic (380) and acidotic, so extra glucose is not the next step (dextrose is added to fluids only once glucose falls during treatment).
key_concept:
DKA = glucose ≥200 mg/dL + pH <7.3 (or HCO3 <15; ISPAD 2022 uses <18) + ketones.
  • Step 1: isotonic IV fluid (cautious volume in children)
  • Step 2: IV regular insulin infusion 0.1 U/kg/h after initial fluids; check K first
  • Add dextrose when glucose falls to about 200-250 mg/dL; keep insulin until acidosis resolves
  • Bicarbonate only in extreme acidosis
  • SC insulin + oral fluids: mild DKA only, alert child, no vomiting
  • Watch for cerebral edema in children
exam_pearl: Vomiting rules out oral rehydration: a vomiting child with pH around 7.1 needs IV fluids and an insulin infusion.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler's typed block highlights C (Subcutaneous insulin + oral hydration) but writes '???' after option B. An embedded screenshot of the same question on p77 prints 'Answer: B' (IV fluid and regular insulin infusion). A separate fuller 'Q:' version (pH 7.0, HCO3 10) is carded separately and highlights IV fluids and insulin infusion.
Other marked answers: Screenshot (p77): B. IV fluid and regular insulin infusion; Compiler '???' mark on B

stem: A 10-year-old child presented to the ER with nausea, vomiting, and deep breathing. Laboratory results: Random blood glucose: 380 mg/dL; ABG: pH = 7.0, HCO3- = 10 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: Glucose 380 mg/dL, "pH = 7.0", "HCO3- = 10", vomiting and deep breathing define severe DKA. The "most appropriate initial management" is IV fluid resuscitation followed by a continuous IV regular insulin infusion, which corrects dehydration, lowers glucose and stops ketogenesis.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV bicarbonate is not routine and in children is linked to cerebral edema and hypokalemia. It is considered only in extreme acidosis (pH below about 6.9) or life-threatening hyperkalemia.
C. Subcutaneous insulin with oral hydration suits only mild DKA in an alert child who tolerates fluids. With pH 7.0 and vomiting, absorption and oral intake are unreliable.
D. Raising bicarbonate does not stop ketosis; only insulin switches off ketone production. This option misunderstands the pathophysiology.
key_concept:
Severe DKA (pH <7.1 or HCO3 <5): IV fluids then IV insulin infusion.
  • Diagnosis: glucose ≥200 mg/dL, pH <7.3 or HCO3 <15 (ISPAD 2022: <18), ketones
  • Fluids first, then regular insulin 0.1 U/kg/h; confirm K is not low before insulin
  • Add dextrose when glucose falls; continue insulin until acidosis resolves
  • No routine bicarbonate
  • Main pediatric risk: cerebral edema
exam_pearl: Bicarbonate is the classic distractor in DKA: insulin, not alkali, clears ketoacidosis.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2536C).
Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 246 (top of p77). Different stem values and options from numbered 246.

stem: 13-year-old obese boy presents with persistent hypertension documented on multiple visits. Examination reveals acanthosis nigricans over the neck and axillae. What is the next step to establish diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: persistent hypertension documented on multiple visits
why_right: An obese 13-year-old with acanthosis nigricans and raised BP on "multiple visits" most likely has primary (obesity-related) hypertension. Before labeling him and starting a workup, the next step "to establish diagnosis" is ambulatory BP monitoring, which confirms sustained hypertension and excludes white coat hypertension.
why_wrong_block:
A. Catecholamines test for pheochromocytoma, which would present with paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations. None are described, and the obesity picture points to primary hypertension.
B. Renal ultrasound looks for renal causes of secondary hypertension, more relevant in young children or with abnormal urinalysis or renal function. It is not the step that confirms the diagnosis of hypertension.
key_concept:
Pediatric hypertension: confirm first, then look for a cause.
  • Age 1 to under 13: BP ≥95th percentile for age, sex and height on ≥3 occasions
  • Age ≥13: adult thresholds
  • ABPM confirms sustained HTN and excludes white coat effect
  • Obese adolescent + acanthosis + family history = primary HTN, insulin resistance
  • Secondary workup (renal, endocrine) if young child, severe HTN or red flags
exam_pearl: "Next step to establish diagnosis" in an asymptomatic obese teen = ABPM, not a hunt for rare secondary causes.

stem: 11year old child with high blood pressure during school screening. Repeat blood pressure measurements above the 95th percentile for age and sex. He has a positive family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus & HTN Examination: weight >95th percentile with acanthosis nigricans "not mentioned that the patient has any symptoms like headache ..." What is the next step to establish diagnosis? • Aldosterone–renin ratio
highlight_terms_source: high blood pressure during school screening
why_right: An 11-year-old with repeated BP "above the 95th percentile", obesity (weight >95th percentile), acanthosis nigricans, family history of T2DM and HTN, and no symptoms fits primary obesity-related hypertension. The next step to establish the diagnosis is ambulatory BP monitoring, which confirms sustained hypertension and rules out white coat hypertension before any secondary workup.
why_wrong_block:
A. Catecholamine levels screen for pheochromocytoma, which presents with paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations. The stem stresses that no such symptoms are present.
B. Renal artery ultrasound looks for renovascular hypertension, suspected with severe HTN, an abdominal bruit or a young non-obese child. It is not a first step in an obese child with a clear primary hypertension profile.
key_concept:
Child with BP ≥95th percentile: confirm with ABPM, then evaluate.
  • Hypertension (1 to under 13 y): ≥95th percentile for age, sex and height on ≥3 occasions
  • ABPM excludes white coat hypertension
  • Obesity + acanthosis + family history = primary HTN
  • Aldosterone-renin ratio: only if hypokalemia or resistant HTN
  • Catecholamines: only with paroxysmal symptoms
exam_pearl: Asymptomatic, obese, family history: confirm with ABPM; secondary causes are chased only when red flags appear.
compiler_note: Compiler note: ABPM confirms true hypertension and avoids misdiagnosis due to white coat effect, especially in children and adolescents; gold standard to confirm persistent hypertension in children before workup. Catecholamine is for pheochromocytoma; not first-line here, no palpitations, headache, sweating. (Stem note: numbers were not given in the recall; 'Aldosterone–renin ratio' appears as an extra choice in the stem.)

stem: 11year old child with high blood pressure during school screening. Repeat blood pressure measurements above the 95th percentile for age and sex. He has a positive family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus & HTN Examination: weight >95th percentile with acanthosis nigricans "not mentioned that the patient has any symptoms like headache ..." What is the next step to establish diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: high blood pressure during school screening
why_wrong_block:
A. Aldosterone-renin ratio screens for primary hyperaldosteronism. It is indicated with hypokalemia or resistant hypertension, neither of which is described here.
B. Catecholamine levels screen for pheochromocytoma. It is indicated with paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations, and the stem notes no such symptoms.
C. Renal artery ultrasound looks for renovascular disease. It is indicated with severe or resistant hypertension, an abdominal bruit or a young non-obese child, not this profile.
D. Cortisol level screens for Cushing syndrome, which would show purple striae, moon face, short stature with weight gain or proximal weakness. Obesity with acanthosis alone suggests insulin resistance, not cortisol excess.
key_concept:
Pediatric HTN: confirm with ABPM before any secondary workup.
  • Definition (1 to under 13 y): ≥95th percentile for age, sex and height on ≥3 occasions
  • Obesity + acanthosis + family history = primary HTN
  • Aldosterone-renin ratio: hypokalemia or resistant HTN
  • Catecholamines: paroxysmal symptoms
  • Cortisol: Cushingoid features (striae, growth failure)
  • Renal or renal artery imaging: young child, severe HTN, bruit or abnormal renal tests
exam_pearl: If the expected answer (ABPM) is missing, do not invent a secondary cause; match each listed test to the red flag that justifies it.
compiler_note: Compiler note: My answer: None of the above are first-line. The next step is to confirm persistent hypertension using Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM). Option D marked with query marks.

stem: IUGR baby with persistent hypothermia was but in a warm area but with no improvement, What is the management?
OptC: Increase ambient temperature and assess after 24 hs
OptD: Emperical antibiotics and full septic workup
why_right: An IUGR neonate with "persistent hypothermia" despite being placed in a warm area, with "no improvement", must be presumed septic. Temperature instability is a common early sign of neonatal sepsis, and IUGR babies are high risk, so the right management is a full septic workup (blood culture, CBC, CRP, with lumbar puncture as indicated) and empirical IV antibiotics without waiting.
why_wrong_block:
A. Glucose infusion treats hypoglycemia, which IUGR babies are prone to and which should be checked. It does not address the persistent hypothermia that points to sepsis.
B. Skin-to-skin contact is a good first measure for simple hypothermia in a stable baby. Here warming has already failed, so a non-environmental cause must be sought.
C. Increasing temperature and waiting 24 hours delays treatment of possible sepsis, which can deteriorate within hours in a neonate. Rewarming alone was already tried.
key_concept:
Neonatal temperature instability (fever or hypothermia) = think sepsis.
  • Hypothermia not correcting with warming is a red flag
  • High risk: preterm, IUGR, low birth weight
  • Workup: blood culture, CBC, CRP, lumbar puncture if indicated
  • Start empirical IV antibiotics while awaiting cultures
  • Also check glucose (IUGR hypoglycemia)
exam_pearl: Simple hypothermia corrects with warming; if it persists despite warming, treat as sepsis now.
compiler_note: Compiler note: UpToDate: temperature instability (fever or hypothermia) in neonates is a common presenting sign of neonatal sepsis; persistent hypothermia despite adequate warming should prompt sepsis evaluation and empiric antibiotics while awaiting cultures. Nelson: hypothermia, lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress are typical signs of neonatal infection, especially in high-risk neonates such as IUGR. Next step: full sepsis workup + empiric IV antibiotics.

stem: Physician had chronic back pain, prescribed himself oxycodone, present to work, agitated and with pinpoint eyes?
OptA: Something related to stress and burn out
why_right: A physician with chronic back pain who is prescribing himself oxycodone and comes to work agitated with pinpoint pupils shows the opioid picture: miosis is the key sign of opioid effect, and self prescription of a controlled drug is a red flag for misuse. This is drug abuse (opioid overuse), not simple burnout.
why_wrong_block:
A. Something related to stress and burn out: burnout causes exhaustion, cynicism and reduced performance, but does not cause pinpoint pupils; it is the distractor that ignores the physical sign.
C. Option not recalled in the source.
D. Option not recalled in the source.
key_concept:
Pupils separate the toxidromes.
  • Pinpoint (< 2 mm): opioids, also organophosphates (with secretions, bradycardia).
  • Dilated: stimulants (cocaine, amphetamine), anticholinergics, opioid withdrawal.
  • Opioid toxicity: miosis, sedation, respiratory depression.
  • Impaired colleague: ensure patient safety and report through proper channels.
exam_pearl: Self prescribed opioid + pinpoint pupils = opioid misuse; withdrawal would give dilated pupils instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Figure: normal constricted pupil 2-4 mm vs pinpoint pupil <2 mm (miosis).

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with a 6-month history of irritability, poor concentration, tension, and anxiety. She is highly active on social media, posting daily. What is the most appropriate initial management?
OptC: Decrease time on the phone to 6 hours
OptD: Encourage her to avoid using social media
why_right: A 17 year old with a 6 month history of irritability, poor concentration, tension and anxiety fits generalized anxiety, linked here to heavy social media use. The lead in is initial management, and in adolescents with anxiety (and no prior treatment) psychological therapy, CBT, is first line before medication.
why_wrong_block:
B. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs): added when symptoms are severe or CBT fails or is unavailable; not the initial step here.
C. Decrease time on the phone to 6 hours: an arbitrary limit that does not treat the anxiety; screen advice is only supportive.
D. Encourage her to avoid using social media: removing a trigger without treating the anxiety, and often rejected by adolescents; not the main management.
key_concept:
Adolescent GAD: CBT first.
  • Generalized anxiety: worry, tension, irritability, poor concentration, sleep problems for ≥ 6 months.
  • Initial: CBT.
  • Severe, or no response to CBT: SSRI.
  • Social media limits: supportive advice only.
exam_pearl: "Initial management" in an untreated adolescent with anxiety is CBT; SSRI is the step after.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other recall: 17-year-old, decreased concentration 6 months, ~9 hours daily on social media, compares herself with others, anxiety and depression, no prior treatment. Options: start antidepressant, force her to leave social media, limit social media time, cognitive behavioral therapy (highlighted).

stem: A mother is worried about her son who has asthma. What is the most appropriate counseling?
OptA: He will develop chronic lung disorder
OptB: Childhood asthma will disappear by adolescence
OptC: He will have asthma for the rest of his life
OptD: No correlation between childhood and adulthood asthma
why_right: The mother asks about her son's future with asthma, so this is a prognosis question. Most children with asthma, especially those with milder or viral-triggered wheeze, become symptom free by adolescence, so the most appropriate counseling is that childhood asthma usually remits as he grows. Persistence into adulthood is the exception and is linked to severe disease, atopy, female sex and parental asthma.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chronic lung disease: well controlled childhood asthma does not usually progress to chronic lung disease; this would only frighten the mother without basis.
C. Lifelong asthma: only a minority remain asthmatic as adults; this would be the prognosis only for severe, atopic disease with strong family history.
D. No correlation: there is a correlation, since severe or atopic childhood asthma increases the chance of persistence or relapse in adulthood.
key_concept:
Childhood asthma prognosis: most children outgrow it.
  • Remission likely: mild disease, viral-triggered wheeze, boys
  • Persistence likely: severe disease, atopy (eczema, allergic rhinitis), female sex, parental asthma
  • Relapse in adulthood is possible even after remission
exam_pearl: Counseling a parent about asthma prognosis: reassure that most outgrow it; the answer flips to persistence only if the stem stresses severe or atopic disease.

stem: 6 month old baby with right esotropia since birth. Absent red light reflex in right eye and negative cover/uncover test. What is the management?
why_right: The decisive clue is an "absent red light reflex in right eye" in a 6-month-old: an abnormal red reflex means leukocoria until proven otherwise, with retinoblastoma and congenital cataract as the key causes. Combined with "right esotropia since birth" (strabismus can be the first sign of a poorly seeing eye), this requires prompt referral to ophthalmology for a dilated eye examination. The negative cover test does not change this, since the red reflex finding alone mandates referral.
why_wrong_block: A. Reassurance is only for pseudostrabismus with a normal, symmetric red reflex and corneal light reflex; an absent red reflex is never normal and may be a malignancy.
key_concept:
Abnormal red reflex in an infant means urgent ophthalmology referral.
  • Leukocoria causes: retinoblastoma, congenital cataract
  • Strabismus may be the presenting sign of retinoblastoma
  • Referral is immediate, not a routine appointment; imaging comes after the dilated exam
  • Untreated strabismus or media opacity leads to amblyopia
exam_pearl: Strabismus plus an absent or white red reflex is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise: refer now, never reassure.

stem: Middle aged man came with metal objects lodged in his eye. What to do next?
highlight_terms_source: metal objects lodged in his eye
why_right: The clue is a metal object lodged in the eye: an embedded or possibly penetrating foreign body is beyond safe removal in a general setting. The correct next step is to leave it in place, protect the eye with a rigid shield (no pressure) and refer urgently to ophthalmology for slit lamp assessment, imaging for retained intraocular metal and removal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Removal and irrigation suit a superficial, loose foreign body or a chemical splash; pulling out a lodged metal object can worsen a penetrating injury and cause extrusion of ocular contents.
C. Antibiotics with clinic follow up fit a simple corneal abrasion after a superficial foreign body has been removed, not an object still embedded in the eye.
D. A pressure patch is avoided in suspected penetrating injury because pressure on the globe can expel contents; a rigid shield is used only as a bridge to referral, not as the management.
key_concept:
Ocular foreign body: superficial and loose = remove/irrigate; embedded or suspected penetrating = do not remove, shield, refer.
  • Superficial FB: topical anaesthetic, irrigate or lift off, then treat as abrasion
  • Embedded or high velocity metal (hammering, grinding): suspect intraocular FB
  • Suspected globe injury: rigid shield, no pressure, no drops, urgent ophthalmology
  • Metal FB imaging: CT orbit (MRI contraindicated)
  • Rust ring after metal FB: removed by ophthalmology
exam_pearl: A lodged or high velocity metal fragment means possible open globe: shield and refer, never pull it out or apply a pressure patch.

stem: Newborn 2 days old came with lethargy, hypotension and pallor. History of Ventose used during delivery. Had head swelling that cross the suture lines. Hb 7.5. Normal platelets normal PTT PT?
highlight_terms_source: head swelling that cross the suture lines
why_right: A 2 day old with lethargy, hypotension and pallor and Hb 7.5 is in hemorrhagic shock. After a vacuum (Ventouse) delivery, a scalp swelling that crosses suture lines and causes this much blood loss fits a subgaleal hemorrhage, a bleed into a large potential space that can hold much of a newborn's blood volume. With normal platelets, PT and PTT this is traumatic bleeding, not a clotting problem, so the priority is to restore volume and oxygen carrying capacity with fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observe with serial Hb: acceptable only for a stable infant with a benign swelling (caput or cephalohematoma) and normal Hb; observing a hypotensive neonate with Hb 7.5 risks death from ongoing bleeding.
C. Vitamin K: treats vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which prolongs the PT; here PT and PTT are normal, so the bleeding is traumatic and vitamin K will not correct shock or anemia.
key_concept:
Neonatal scalp swellings after instrumental delivery:
  • Caput succedaneum: soft scalp edema, crosses sutures, largest at birth, resolves within days, no significant blood loss
  • Cephalohematoma: subperiosteal blood, limited by sutures, grows after birth, resolves over months, may cause jaundice
  • Subgaleal hemorrhage: crosses sutures, boggy and expanding, typical after vacuum, can cause hypovolemic shock
  • Shock + low Hb + normal coagulation = transfuse and resuscitate
exam_pearl: Caput also crosses sutures but never causes shock; a swelling that crosses sutures with pallor, hypotension and falling Hb is subgaleal hemorrhage and needs urgent resuscitation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Hb 7.5 is severe anemia for a newborn; vacuum delivery = birth trauma risk; swelling crossing sutures (compiler: caput succedaneum); lethargy, hypotension, pallor = significant blood loss; normal coagulation = not vitamin K deficiency bleeding. Severely anemic symptomatic neonate requires urgent transfusion and fluid resuscitation. Observation unsafe; vitamin K unnecessary. Nelson: hemodynamically unstable newborns with Hb <8 need transfusion.

stem: Elderly patient in 70s, Hx of HTN, brought by his son. He stated to forget recent events but remembers old events. He forgets names. He misplaces his items and can't find them, social activities withdrawal due to lack of interest. Minimental exam was done and the result was low (I can't remember exactly the number). On MRI: there was cortical atrophy. What medication to start?
highlight_terms_source: forget recent events but remembers old events
why_right: An elderly man with recent memory loss but preserved remote memory, forgetting names, misplacing items, withdrawal, a low MMSE and cortical atrophy on MRI has Alzheimer disease. The lead-in asks which medication to start, and first-line drug therapy for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease is a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine), which modestly improves or stabilises cognition and function.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antipsychotics do not treat the cognitive deficit and raise mortality in elderly patients with dementia; they are reserved for severe psychosis or agitation that endangers the patient or others.
B. His withdrawal reflects apathy from dementia, not a depressive episode; an antidepressant is right when there are core depressive features (low mood, guilt) or pseudodementia, not progressive amnestic decline with atrophy.
key_concept:
Alzheimer disease: recent memory lost first, remote memory kept, progressive decline; treat with a cholinesterase inhibitor.
  • Mild to moderate: donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine
  • Moderate to severe: add or use memantine (NMDA antagonist)
  • Imaging first to exclude structural causes; Alzheimer shows cortical and hippocampal atrophy
  • Benign forgetfulness: does not impair daily function
  • Antipsychotics only for dangerous psychosis or agitation
exam_pearl: Social withdrawal in dementia is usually apathy; do not let it pull you toward an antidepressant when the picture is amnestic decline with atrophy.

stem: 25 y/o has difficulty with sleep, sleepy on afternoons. Works on his computer programming at night, has irregular sleep schedule. What to do?
OptB: Regular sleep schedule and limit screen time
highlight_terms_source: difficulty with sleep, sleepy on afternoons
why_right: A young programmer who works at night with an irregular sleep schedule and afternoon sleepiness has a behavioural and circadian problem driven by poor sleep hygiene and evening screen light. The first step is to correct the cause: fix a regular sleep and wake time and limit screen exposure before bed.
why_wrong_block: A. CBT for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder (difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on most nights for about 3 months despite adequate opportunity); here the problem is a self-imposed irregular schedule, so simple sleep hygiene comes first.
key_concept:
Sleep complaint from an irregular, night-time, screen-heavy routine = fix sleep hygiene first.
  • Fixed wake time and bedtime, including weekends
  • Limit screens and bright light before bed
  • Avoid caffeine later in the day and long daytime naps
  • Chronic insomnia disorder (about 3 months) = CBT-I first line
  • Hypnotics are short term only, never first line
exam_pearl: Clear behavioural trigger (night work, irregular hours, screens) points to sleep hygiene; a documented chronic insomnia disorder points to CBT-I.

stem: A 2-day-old infant weighing 5.2 kg at birth presents with hypoglycaemia but is feeding well. The mother had gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and was treated with insulin during pregnancy. What is the most likely cause of the infant's hypoglycaemia?
highlight_terms_source: gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and was treated with insulin
why_right: The clues are a macrosomic baby (5.2 kg) of a mother with GDM on insulin. Maternal hyperglycemia crosses the placenta, the fetal pancreas responds with beta cell hyperplasia and high insulin output, and this drives fetal overgrowth. After the cord is cut the maternal glucose supply stops but the high insulin persists, so the infant becomes hypoglycemic despite feeding well: transient neonatal hyperinsulinemia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Organic acidemia: presents with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, metabolic acidosis and ketosis in a sick neonate, not hypoglycemia in a well fed macrosomic infant of a diabetic mother.
C. Adrenal insufficiency: suggested by hypoglycemia with salt wasting (low Na, high K), ambiguous genitalia in a girl (CAH) or shock; nothing here points to it.
D. Glucagon deficiency: a very rare isolated cause; maternal diabetes and macrosomia point clearly to excess fetal insulin, not lack of counter-regulatory hormone.
key_concept:
Infant of a diabetic mother: fetal hyperinsulinemia explains most complications.
  • Macrosomia and shoulder dystocia
  • Neonatal hypoglycemia (persistent insulin after cord clamping)
  • RDS (insulin delays surfactant maturation)
  • Polycythemia and hyperbilirubinemia
  • Hypocalcemia
exam_pearl: Big baby + diabetic mother + hypoglycemia despite good feeding = hyperinsulinemia; a sick, acidotic, poorly feeding neonate points to an inborn error instead.

stem: A child presents with an asymptomatic flank swelling that is hard and non-tender. An abdominal X-ray shows a soft-tissue mass with calcification. What is the next step in management?
why_right: A child with a hard, non-tender flank mass and calcification on X-ray suggests neuroblastoma (calcification is common in neuroblastoma and uncommon in Wilms tumor). The next step is cross-sectional imaging to define the mass: its organ of origin, extent, vessel involvement and spread. Contrast CT of the abdomen shows calcification well and stages the tumor, so it is the keyed next step before tissue diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal MRI: also an accepted staging study (no radiation, good for spinal extension) and preferred at some centers, but CT is the classic exam answer and shows calcification better.
C. Biopsy: tissue diagnosis comes only after imaging has defined the mass and its organ of origin; a suspected Wilms tumor is usually not biopsied upfront at all, because biopsy can spill tumor and upstage it.
key_concept:
Pediatric abdominal mass: image first, tissue later.
  • Neuroblastoma: hard, irregular, may cross midline, calcification, raised urinary VMA/HVA, child often unwell
  • Wilms tumor: smooth flank mass, does not cross midline, rarely calcified, child usually well
  • Sequence: ultrasound, then CT or MRI, then tissue diagnosis
exam_pearl: Calcified flank mass in a child = think neuroblastoma; the next step is CT, not biopsy first.

stem: A preterm infant born at 29 weeks presents with tachypnea, grunting, and nasal flaring, indicating respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A 29 week preterm with tachypnea, grunting and nasal flaring has RDS, caused by surfactant deficiency. Exogenous surfactant treats the underlying cause, improves lung compliance and reduces mortality and air leak, so it is the most appropriate management here. Of the two options, it is the only one that is correct as written.
why_wrong_block: A. CPAP with 100% oxygen: CPAP is a valid first support in a spontaneously breathing preterm, but routine 100% oxygen is wrong because preterm infants need oxygen titrated to target saturations to avoid hyperoxia injury such as retinopathy of prematurity.
key_concept:
Neonatal RDS: surfactant deficiency in preterm infants.
  • Clues: preterm, distress from birth, grunting, flaring, retractions
  • CXR: diffuse ground glass (reticulogranular) with air bronchograms
  • Management: CPAP support plus surfactant when oxygen needs are rising, oxygen titrated to targets
  • Prevention: antenatal corticosteroids
  • TTN instead: term, C-section, fluid in fissures, self-resolving
exam_pearl: Preterm + grunting = RDS: give surfactant; any option with 100% oxygen in a preterm is a trap.

stem: (...) year old child presents with 2 months history of epigastric pain that wakes him up at night, mother mentioned a History of PUD, what is the confirmatory test?
highlight_terms_source: epigastric pain that wakes him up at night
why_right: Two months of epigastric pain that wakes him at night with a family history of PUD suggests peptic ulcer disease, often with H. pylori. The lead-in asks for the confirmatory test: only upper GI endoscopy shows the ulcer directly, and biopsy confirms H. pylori and excludes other pathology. Noninvasive tests can suggest H. pylori but cannot confirm an ulcer.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC: may show anemia from chronic blood loss, but it is nonspecific and cannot confirm an ulcer.
B. Abdominal ultrasound: useful for gallstones, pancreatic or hepatic disease, but it cannot see the gastric or duodenal mucosa.
D. H. pylori stool antigen only: detects infection and is mainly used to confirm eradication after treatment; it cannot show an ulcer, and in children diagnosis should be by endoscopy with biopsy rather than a noninvasive test alone.
key_concept:
Suspected PUD in a child:
  • Clues: epigastric pain waking at night, family history, hematemesis or melena
  • Confirm: upper GI endoscopy with biopsy (ulcer + H. pylori histology/culture)
  • Noninvasive tests (urea breath test, stool antigen): mainly to confirm eradication; not for initial diagnosis in children
  • Treat H. pylori: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin; quadruple therapy if failed
exam_pearl: "Confirmatory" for PUD = endoscopy with biopsy; urea breath test or stool antigen are the answer when the question asks how to confirm eradication.

stem: A 3-month-old infant with noisy breath since birth change with positioning; disappears in prone position and become more obvious with supine position. Examination and growth parameter are normal. The mother concerned about this sound. Which of the following is the most appropriate counselling should be given?
OptD: Will improve by her first birthday
highlight_terms_source: disappears in prone position and become more obvious with supine position
Examination and growth parameter are normal
why_right: Noisy breathing since birth that disappears prone and is worse supine with normal growth and examination is laryngomalacia: floppy supraglottic tissue collapses on inspiration. It is self-limiting and usually resolves by 1 to 2 years, so the correct counselling is reassurance that it will improve by her first birthday.
why_wrong_block:
A. Will worsen with time: the noise may peak in the first months but laryngomalacia does not progressively worsen; it improves as the airway matures.
B. Needs surgical correction: supraglottoplasty is reserved for severe disease with failure to thrive, apnea, cyanosis or feeding difficulty; this infant is thriving.
C. Normal developmental sounds: the noise comes from a structural airway disorder (laryngomalacia), even though it is benign; calling it normal skips the diagnosis and the expected course.
key_concept:
Congenital stridor by position:
  • Better prone, worse supine = laryngomalacia (diagnosis: laryngoscopy)
  • Better supine = tracheomalacia (diagnosis: bronchoscopy)
  • Both self-limiting, resolve by 1 to 2 years
  • Red flags for surgery: failure to thrive, apnea, cyanosis, feeding problems
exam_pearl: Thriving infant with positional stridor: reassure; the answer flips to surgery only if growth falters or there are apneas or cyanosis.

stem: Meconium aspiration with severe respiratory distress. What to do?
why_right: Meconium aspiration with severe respiratory distress means respiratory failure: meconium blocks airways, inactivates surfactant and causes chemical pneumonitis and often pulmonary hypertension. A neonate in severe distress cannot be supported by supplemental oxygen alone, so the next step is to secure the airway with intubation and provide mechanical ventilation (with surfactant and treatment of pulmonary hypertension as needed).
why_wrong_block:
A. Mask oxygen: fits mild distress with adequate effort; it does not support ventilation or provide pressure in severe distress.
C. Low-flow oxygen: suitable only for mild hypoxemia without significant distress; it is inadequate for a neonate in respiratory failure.
key_concept:
Meconium aspiration syndrome:
  • Risk: post-term, fetal distress, meconium-stained liquor
  • Vigorous baby: routine care, no tracheal suctioning
  • Non-vigorous baby: start resuscitation with PPV; routine tracheal suctioning is no longer recommended
  • Severe distress or respiratory failure: intubation and mechanical ventilation, surfactant, treat pulmonary hypertension (inhaled nitric oxide, ECMO if refractory)
  • CXR: patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation
exam_pearl: Severity decides support: mild distress gets oxygen, severe distress gets intubation and ventilation.

stem: A 2-month-old baby (chronological age) born at 34 weeks gestation. Mother presents to the clinic for immunization.
why_right: A 34 week baby who is now 2 months chronological age gets the standard 2-month vaccines today. Preterm infants are immunized according to chronological age with full doses, because their immune response at that age is adequate and delaying leaves them unprotected when they are most vulnerable.
why_wrong_block:
B. Prematurity schedule (corrected age): corrected age is used for growth and developmental assessment, not vaccine timing; there is no separate delayed schedule for preterm infants.
C. Immunize for 6 months: giving the 6-month vaccines now would be too early and skips the 2 and 4 month doses; the schedule follows actual age.
key_concept:
Preterm vaccination rule:
  • Timing: chronological age
  • Dose: full dose, never reduced
  • Corrected age: growth and development only (until about 2 years)
  • Exception: hepatitis B birth dose in infants under 2 kg depends on maternal HBsAg status
exam_pearl: Vaccines follow chronological age; milestones and growth follow corrected age.

stem: A hypertensive man presents with a bright red spot in the eye. No pain, no vision change, no infection signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: bright red spot in the eye
why_right: A bright red, well demarcated patch on the white of the eye with no pain, no visual change and no discharge is the classic subconjunctival hemorrhage. Hypertension is a recognised risk factor (fragile conjunctival vessels), along with straining, coughing, trauma and anticoagulant or antiplatelet use. It is benign and resolves on its own over about 2 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Conjunctivitis gives diffuse redness with discharge, grittiness or itch, usually bilateral; here there are no infection signs and the redness is a solid spot.
B. Scleritis causes severe, boring pain (often waking the patient), tenderness and a deep violaceous hue, and can threaten vision; this patient has no pain.
C. Episcleritis gives sectoral pinkish redness of dilated vessels with mild discomfort; it is engorged vessels, not a flat sheet of blood obscuring the sclera.
key_concept:
Painless red eye with a flat bright red patch, normal vision, no discharge = subconjunctival hemorrhage.
  • Risks: hypertension, Valsalva/cough, trauma, anticoagulants or antiplatelets, bleeding disorders
  • Management: reassure, check BP; resolves over about 2 weeks
  • Recurrent: check BP, INR or bleeding screen
  • Traumatic with no posterior limit: think orbital or skull base fracture
exam_pearl: Pain or reduced vision with a red eye points away from subconjunctival hemorrhage toward scleritis, keratitis, uveitis or glaucoma.

stem: Child fell down then had tonic-clonic seizure, came to the ER, drowsy but rousable, neurological exam is normal (includes pupils etc.). Best step:
why_right: A child who "fell" and then had a tonic-clonic seizure and is now "drowsy but rousable" has two high-risk features after head trauma: a post-traumatic seizure and altered mental status (drowsiness counts even with a normal focal exam). These place the child in the group needing urgent non-contrast head CT to exclude an intracranial bleed. Non-contrast CT is the fastest test to show acute blood, and a normal pupil and limb exam does not exclude a hematoma.
why_wrong_block: B. Admit for observation 24 hours: observation alone suits a child with minor head injury, normal mental status and only intermediate features (brief vomiting, headache, no LOC). A post-traumatic seizure with drowsiness needs imaging first; observation follows a normal CT.
key_concept:
Pediatric head trauma: image when high-risk features are present, observe when only intermediate features exist.
  • CT now: altered mental status or GCS <15, post-traumatic seizure, signs of skull base or depressed fracture, focal deficit
  • Observation vs CT: brief LOC, vomiting, severe headache, severe mechanism, with normal mental status
  • Neither: minor mechanism, normal child
  • CT is non-contrast (blood is bright on plain CT); MRI is not first-line acutely
exam_pearl: A normal neuro exam does not cancel CT if the child seized after the fall or is drowsy; those features alone mandate imaging.

stem: Bronchiolitis typical symptoms. Next step?
OptA: High flow O2 and IV fluids
OptB: Low flow O2, supportive care, suction
why_right: Bronchiolitis (usually RSV) is a self-limiting viral illness with no curative drug, so management is supportive: oxygen if saturation is low, nasal suctioning to clear the airway (infants are obligate nose breathers), and maintaining hydration and feeding. For a "typical" case without signs of severe distress or fatigue, low flow oxygen is the right level of support.
why_wrong_block: A. High flow O2 and IV fluids: an escalation step for severe disease (marked work of breathing, persistent hypoxia on low flow, apnea, or inability to feed). Not the starting point for a typical case.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis = clinical diagnosis; treatment = oxygen + hydration + suction, escalated by severity.
  • Mild: home, nasal suction, small frequent feeds
  • Moderate (hypoxia, tachypnea, poor feeding): admit, low flow O2, NG or IV fluids if not feeding
  • Severe/failing: high flow, CPAP/NIV in PICU
  • Not routinely used: bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics, routine CXR
exam_pearl: Apnea in a young infant or rising work of breathing despite low flow oxygen flips management to high flow/NIV and critical care.

stem: Child with sore throat for 2 days. Exam: enlarged tonsils with exudate, pharyngeal petechiae, anterior and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Rapid strep positive. T = 39°C. Others normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Fever of 39°C, tonsillar exudate and cervical nodes with a "rapid strep positive" result confirms group A streptococcal pharyngitis; no further test is needed. The next step is antibiotic treatment, and oral penicillin V for a full 10-day course is first line (amoxicillin is an accepted equivalent). The full course is what prevents acute rheumatic fever.
why_wrong_block:
B. Throat culture: the back-up test when the rapid antigen test is NEGATIVE in a child with a suggestive picture. A positive rapid test is specific enough to treat without culture.
C. Reassurance: appropriate for viral pharyngitis (mild hyperemia, negative rapid test). Confirmed GAS needs antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever and suppurative complications.
D. This option was blank in the recall and carries no content.
key_concept:
Sore throat in a child: test before treating, treat only confirmed GAS.
  • Suggestive picture: rapid antigen detection test first
  • RADT positive: treat (penicillin V or amoxicillin, 10 days)
  • RADT negative in a child: confirm with throat culture
  • Penicillin allergy: macrolide or cephalosporin by allergy type
  • Asymptomatic contacts: observe, no prophylaxis
exam_pearl: Exudate with posterior cervical nodes also fits EBV mononucleosis; the positive rapid strep settles it as GAS here, but if EBV is likely, amoxicillin often provokes a widespread rash.

stem: A 6-year-old child seen at pre-school screening clinic. What are the recommended vaccines at this stage according to national program in Saudi Arabia?
why_right: At pre-school / primary school entry the Saudi national schedule gives the booster set: OPV, DTaP, MMR and varicella. This is exactly option C. The "6-year-old" at school screening is the cue for the school-entry visit.
why_wrong_block:
A. MMR.DTP.OPV: incomplete; it leaves out varicella, which is also given at school entry.
B. MMR.HBV.DTP.HAV: hepatitis B is completed in infancy and hepatitis A at 18 and 24 months, so neither belongs at school entry; varicella and OPV are missing.
D. MMR.varicella.OPV.PCV: PCV is an infant series vaccine (2, 4, 6, 12 months) and is not routine in a healthy 6-year-old; DTP is missing.
key_concept:
Saudi schedule anchor visits:
  • Birth: BCG, Hep B
  • 2, 4 months: IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV, rotavirus
  • 6 months: OPV, IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV
  • 9 months: measles, MCV4; 12 months: OPV, MMR, PCV, MCV4
  • 18 months: OPV, DTaP, Hib, MMR, varicella, Hep A; 24 months: Hep A
  • School entry: OPV, DTaP, MMR, varicella
exam_pearl: School entry repeats the 18-month boosters minus Hib and Hep A: OPV, DTaP, MMR, varicella.

stem: Name of the reflex? (in the picture)
why_right: The picture shows a finger stroking the newborn's cheek with the mouth opening and turning toward it. Turning the head and mouth toward a touch at the side of the mouth is the rooting reflex, present from birth and fading by about 4 months.
why_wrong_block: B. Suckling: the sucking reflex is triggered by something placed INSIDE the mouth or touching the palate, producing rhythmic sucking; stroking the cheek causes rooting, not sucking.
key_concept:
Mouth reflexes of the newborn:
  • Rooting: stroke cheek or corner of mouth, head turns and mouth opens toward stimulus; gone by about 4 months
  • Sucking: object in mouth or on palate, rhythmic sucking
  • Both help feeding; absence suggests CNS depression
exam_pearl: Cheek touched = rooting; object in the mouth = sucking.

stem: 2 month old; his mother mentioned she noticed his right eye goes inward while feeding, she's concerned. What's the most initial management? (Esotropia)
why_right: The clues are age 2 months and an eye that turns inward only while feeding, i.e. intermittent. Binocular control is still immature in the first few months, so intermittent misalignment is normal and the initial management is to reassure the mother and re-examine at follow up.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT is not used to assess infant ocular alignment; imaging is reserved for abnormal findings such as leukocoria, proptosis or neurological signs.
B. Ophthalmology referral is right for a constant deviation at any age, a deviation persisting beyond about 4 to 6 months, an abnormal red reflex or an asymmetric corneal light reflex.
key_concept:
Infant eye alignment: intermittent misalignment in the first months is normal; constant or persistent deviation is not.
  • Under about 4 months, intermittent, normal red reflex: reassure and recheck
  • Constant deviation at any age: refer
  • Any deviation persisting after about 4 to 6 months: refer (amblyopia risk)
  • Abnormal or absent red reflex: urgent referral (retinoblastoma, cataract)
  • Symmetric corneal light reflex with apparent squint: pseudostrabismus (epicanthal folds)
exam_pearl: Same infant with a constant inward turn, or still deviating after about 4 to 6 months, needs referral, not reassurance.

stem: 6-Year-Old Bedwetting, Never Been Dry At Night, His Brother Had The Same Problem. Next Step?
why_right: A 6-year-old who has never been dry at night has primary nocturnal enuresis, and a sibling with the same problem shows the strong familial tendency. At this age bedwetting is still common and resolves spontaneously in most children each year, so the first step is reassurance with simple behavioural advice (no punishment, voiding before bed, limiting evening fluids).
why_wrong_block:
B. Desmopressin is for older children when behavioural measures and the alarm fail, or for short-term needs such as sleepovers; it is not the first step at 6.
C. Toilet training addresses daytime continence, which is usually already achieved; nighttime dryness depends on bladder maturation and ADH rhythm, not training.
D. The enuresis alarm is the most effective active treatment once a motivated older child and family want treatment after behavioural measures; it is not the first step here.
key_concept:
Primary nocturnal enuresis:
  • Bedwetting is considered significant after about 6 years
  • Strong family history; spontaneous resolution each year
  • Ladder: reassurance and behavioural measures → enuresis alarm → desmopressin (oral, not intranasal)
  • Secondary enuresis (previously dry) or daytime symptoms: look for UTI, diabetes, constipation, stress
exam_pearl: Never dry + family history + young age = reassure; new bedwetting after being dry = investigate (urinalysis, glucose).

stem: A 3-year-old child Play Alone, obeys complex commands, pours water from a pitcher, but cannot draw a circle. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
why_right: At 3 years the child "obeys complex commands" (receptive language on track) and "pours water from a pitcher" (good fine motor and self-help control). In the milestone table used for this exam, copying a circle is a 4-year skill, so not drawing one yet is not a delay, and playing alone (solitary or parallel play) is still common at this age. With no domain clearly behind and no gross motor problem described, the profile is read as normal for age.
why_wrong_block:
B. Psychosocial development delay: would need clear social red flags (no interest in peers, no pretend play, poor eye contact, loss of skills). "Plays alone" by itself, with intact comprehension, is not enough.
C. Gross motor delay: no gross motor finding is given (walking, running, stairs, tricycle); pouring water and drawing are fine motor tasks.
D. This option was not recalled ("Forget") and carries no content.
key_concept:
Judge development by domain, and call delay only when a domain misses its expected age.
  • 3 years: stairs with alternating feet, tricycle, 3-word sentences, speech 75% intelligible, uses spoon well, parallel play moving to group play
  • 4 years: hops on one foot, copies a circle (per this table), draws person with 3 parts, tells stories
  • 5 years: copies a square; 6 years: copies a triangle
exam_pearl: Check which domain the missing skill belongs to: an isolated fine motor item with everything else normal does not make a gross motor or global delay.

stem: Pediatric girl with diabetes uncontrolled, her glucose was high. What to do? The stem was something education promotion preventive bla bla.
OptA: Teach family how to insulin use and diet basics
OptB: Give them pamphlet and arrange follow up
OptC: Refer him to somewhere I don't remember (in my exam)
why_right: Poor glycemic control in a child with diabetes is most often due to gaps in day-to-day self-management, and the stem frames the question as education / health promotion. The most effective step is direct, hands-on education of the family: insulin technique and dosing, glucose monitoring, diet basics, and recognizing and treating hypoglycemia. Active teaching with return demonstration changes behavior; passive measures do not.
why_wrong_block:
B. Give them pamphlet and arrange follow up: written material alone is passive and does not check understanding or skill; it supplements but does not replace face-to-face teaching.
C. Refer him to somewhere (not recalled): referral may help if specialist or psychosocial issues exist, but the first step in a health-promotion question is to educate the family yourself.
key_concept:
Uncontrolled pediatric diabetes: find and fix the self-management gap first.
  • Teach insulin injection, dosing and site rotation
  • Glucose monitoring and sick-day rules
  • Diet basics (carbohydrate awareness, regular meals)
  • Hypoglycemia recognition and treatment (most important insulin adverse effect)
  • Involve the whole family and school
exam_pearl: In "education / promotion" questions, active teaching of the family beats pamphlets or referral.

stem: Newborn stepping reflex (shown in images). Time of disappearance?
why_right: The stepping (walking) reflex is present at birth and is one of the earliest primitive reflexes to fade, usually disappearing by about 2 months. That makes "by 2 months" the correct disappearance age.
why_wrong_block:
B. By 4 months: the typical disappearance age of the rooting and Galant (trunk incurvation) reflexes, not stepping.
C. By 6 months: the disappearance age of the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes.
key_concept:
Primitive reflex disappearance ages:
  • About 2 months: stepping; ATNR about 2 to 3 months
  • About 4 months: rooting, Galant; placing 4 to 6 months
  • About 6 months: Moro, palmar grasp
  • 12 to 18 months: Babinski
  • Parachute appears at 8 to 10 months and persists for life
exam_pearl: Reflexes that persist well beyond their expected age suggest CNS pathology such as cerebral palsy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Second question from the same unnumbered reflex screenshot; bold option taken as marked answer.

stem: A newborn is delivered with cleft palate, micrognathia, and glossoptosis. He has difficulty suckling and breathing, is partially fed via NG tube, and experiences random episodes of apnea. What is the most appropriate management?
OptA: Refer to ENT and continue NG tube feeding until ENT evaluation
OptB: Refer for sleep study and provide NG tube feeding for evaluation of breathing
OptC: Refer for palate surgery and respiratory monitoring
OptD: Counsel cardio and genetics while maintaining NGT for feeding
key_concept:
Pierre Robin sequence: micrognathia → glossoptosis → upper airway obstruction (often with cleft palate).
  • First: airway (prone or lateral positioning, nasopharyngeal airway, airway/ENT team)
  • Feeding: special cleft feeders or NG tube; monitor weight
  • Sleep study to grade obstruction once stable
  • Severe or refractory: mandibular distraction or tongue lip adhesion; tracheostomy rarely
  • Genetics: screen for Stickler, 22q11 deletion
  • Palate repair is delayed to later infancy
exam_pearl: Apnea in Pierre Robin is obstructive from the tongue, so the airway team comes before the palate surgeon.
